225. ASYMMETRIC DETECTION EFFICIENCIES

The symmetric eta threshold is not the whole loss story.

For certain two-party dichotomic loss models, a necessary threshold relation can be written in a form such as
    eta_A + eta_B < 3 eta_A eta_B
for Bell violation to remain possible under the optimized scenario.

If one side is effectively perfect,
    eta_A=1,
then
    1+eta_B < 3 eta_B
implies
    eta_B>1/2.

This motivates hybrid architectures in which one subsystem has near-unit readout efficiency while the remote photonic channel bears most of the loss.

Threshold warning:
The exact inequality, state, background, heralding, and measurement architecture still matter. Do not quote 50% as a universal asymmetric threshold.

226. LOSS IS NOT IDENTICAL TO CHANNEL TRANSMISSION

Overall efficiency can combine:
- source coupling probability;
- channel transmission;
- collection efficiency;
- detector quantum efficiency;
- analysis optics;
- heralding success;
- electronic acceptance.

An experiment may call some losses "preparation failure" and others "detection loss" depending on where the trial is defined.

This classification is legitimate only if the herald/trial definition is independent of the later Bell choices in the manner required by the theorem.

227. EVENT-READY HERALDING AND THE DETECTION LOOPHOLE

A herald can move some loss outside the Bell trial:
Only after a successful entanglement-generation herald is a Bell trial declared.

This can be valid because the setting choices for the Bell measurement are made after the herald, so the herald cannot select on those future settings under the assumed causal structure.

If settings are already known before heralding, or if herald acceptance depends on them, the argument changes.

The temporal order is therefore part of the theorem implementation.

228. LOCALITY OF THE OUTCOME EVENT

In a real detector, when is an outcome "fixed"?

Candidates:
- microscopic absorption;
- avalanche onset;
- threshold crossing;
- digital registration;
- macroscopic amplification.

Different interpretations of measurement may place the physically relevant event at different stages.

Experimental Bell papers usually define an operational event based on electronics and ensure spacelike separation for that event with conservative margins.

This is sufficient for testing ordinary signal models tied to that operational definition, but philosophical collapse models may pose additional questions beyond standard Bell statistics.

229. BELL'S THEOREM VERSUS EARLIER HIDDEN-VARIABLE NO-GO THEOREMS

Earlier impossibility arguments, notably von Neumann's, attempted to constrain hidden-variable completions without using Bell's spacelike locality structure.

Bell later criticized assumptions in such arguments and emphasized that hidden-variable theories such as Bohm's explicitly exist.

Bell's distinctive theorem is therefore not:
"hidden variables are impossible."

It is:
"local hidden-variable completions satisfying the Bell assumptions cannot reproduce all quantum correlations."

This historical contrast is essential.

230. BELL VERSUS KOCHEN-SPECKER

Kochen-Specker contextuality, developed after Bell's 1964 work, rules out broad classes of noncontextual value assignments in Hilbert spaces of dimension at least three.

Bell nonlocality uses spatially separated measurement choices to motivate a particular context-independence/locality condition and yields inequalities directly testable with separated parties.

The theorems are related but not interchangeable.

231. REICHENBACH-STYLE COMMON-CAUSE MOTIVATION

A classical common-cause intuition says that correlations between spacelike separated outcomes should be explainable by variables in their shared past.

A sufficiently complete common cause should screen off the correlation when conditioned upon.

Bell factorization can be viewed as a sharpened, setting-sensitive version of this idea.

The theorem then says:
the quantum correlation pattern does not admit such a local screening-off explanation under measurement independence.

232. "COMPLETE LAMBDA" DOES NOT MEAN ONTOLOGICALLY COMPLETE UNIVERSE

Lambda need only be complete relative to the candidate causal explanation:
it should include all variables the model says are relevant common causes for the outcomes.

If an omitted variable remains correlated with both wings, append it to lambda.

The theorem quantifies over arbitrary lambda spaces, so making lambda richer does not evade the inequality as long as factorization and setting independence are retained.

233. STOCHASTIC INSTRUMENT VARIABLES

Real apparatuses have local noise variables:
    mu_A, mu_B.

These can be included in local response functions or absorbed into an enlarged lambda when appropriate.

If they are generated locally after settings are chosen and independently across wings, they do not help violate CHSH under locality.

If they are correlated across wings or with settings, their causal role must be represented explicitly.

234. TIME-DEPENDENT HIDDEN VARIABLES

A local model can allow lambda_i to evolve with trial index and depend on previous local history.

Bell analysis does not require a timeless fixed instruction table across the entire experiment.

Per-trial factorization plus valid setting independence can still imply a sequential Bell bound.

This is why memory-robust statistics are so important.

235. SOURCE DRIFT DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY VIOLATE THE THEOREM

If rho_i(lambda) changes slowly with time but settings are randomized independently on each trial, every setting pair samples the time-varying source approximately according to the randomization schedule.

A sequential Bell proof can permit rho_i to depend on the past.

The dangerous case is not drift itself but drift combined with predictable/block-structured settings or postselection that makes different setting pairs sample systematically different source states.

236. NO-SIGNALLING FINITE-SAMPLE TEST

For each Alice setting x, compare Alice's outcome distribution across Bob's y values.

A simple difference:
    Delta_x =
      P_hat(A=+1|x,y=0)
      -P_hat(A=+1|x,y=1).

Under ideal no-signalling, Delta_x=0 in the population.

Finite sample analysis should:
- use an appropriate contingency-table or likelihood test;
- account for multiple x and Bob-side comparisons;
- distinguish statistical fluctuation from physical setting leakage.

A significant marginal anomaly is an apparatus diagnostic, not automatically evidence for controllable superluminal signalling.

237. LOCAL FRACTION / NONLOCAL CONTENT

One can ask whether a behavior can be decomposed as
    P = p P_local + (1-p) P_nonlocal
under a specified larger model set.

The maximum p is sometimes called a local fraction in a chosen framework.

This gives a graded measure of how much local behavior can be mixed into the observed correlations, rather than a binary "violates/does not violate" statement.

It is an optimization problem and depends on the allowed nonlocal remainder.

238. DISTANCE-BASED ROBUSTNESS TO THE LOCAL SET

Given an empirical table with noise, solve
    min_{Q in Local} D(P_hat,Q)
for a statistical distance D.

Choices:
- total variation;
- Euclidean distance;
- KL divergence/relative entropy;
- likelihood loss.

The nearest local model can be useful for:
- effect-size interpretation;
- designing a likelihood-ratio test;
- identifying which probabilities drive the violation.

239. BELL INEQUALITY OPTIMIZATION FOR A KNOWN EXPERIMENTAL NOISE MODEL

If the state and detector model are approximately known:
1. predict the full behavior P_theta;
2. estimate the local polytope;
3. optimize a Bell functional for statistical separation between P_theta and Local;
4. include loss and setting probabilities;
5. verify robustness across uncertainty in theta.

This can outperform blindly using canonical CHSH settings.

240. AVOID CIRCULAR OPTIMIZATION ON THE TEST DATA

If the Bell inequality itself is optimized using the same finite dataset later used to claim significance, the local-null p-value must account for that optimization.

Better:
- optimize using theory/calibration/training data;
- freeze the inequality;
- evaluate on held-out test data.

Prediction-based-ratio methods can adapt sequentially when the adaptation is constructed to preserve validity.

241. EXPERIMENTAL POWER ANALYSIS

Before running:
- specify expected quantum behavior;
- specify conservative efficiency/background/timing parameters;
- simulate the chosen statistical test;
- estimate trials required for target evidence;
- examine sensitivity to drift and setting bias.

This is a power calculation, not a p-value after the fact.

242. RESEARCH DECISION RULE FOR A NONVIOLATION

If no statistically secure Bell violation is observed, do not conclude "local realism is true."

Possible causes:
- insufficient entanglement visibility;
- detector loss;
- background;
- wrong settings;
- low sample size;
- calibration errors;
- real disagreement with the quantum model.

The next step is model discrimination and systematics diagnosis, not inversion of the theorem.

243. RESEARCH DECISION RULE FOR A VIOLATION

If a violation is observed:
1. verify sign convention and raw counts;
2. verify loss/trial handling;
3. verify setting independence assumptions;
4. verify spacetime separation;
5. run memory-valid statistics;
6. audit multiple testing/stopping;
7. examine no-signalling diagnostics;
8. reproduce with independent code;
9. compare with quantum prediction;
10. only then make foundational claims.

244. WHY BELL THEORY IS A MODEL OF SCIENTIFIC MATURITY

The progression is exemplary:
- conceptual puzzle;
- mathematical model class;
- inequality;
- optimized quantum counterexample;
- experiment;
- loophole analysis;
- statistics;
- convex geometry;
- information-theoretic applications;
- causal generalization.

At every stage, the field learned to replace a vague objection with a more explicit assumption or measurable quantity.

245. FINAL RESEARCH-GRADE CONCLUSION

The mature statement is not:
"Quantum mechanics is spooky."

It is:
Observed Bell-test behaviors violate inequalities satisfied by every model in a precisely defined local latent-variable class, under quantified assumptions about setting independence and the mapping from physical trials to mathematical variables. Quantum theory predicts the violations and bounds them by its own stronger constraint, while operational no-signalling remains intact.

That statement is simultaneously mathematically sharp, experimentally testable, statistically auditable, and interpretation-neutral.
</think>

Bell's theorem is a family of impossibility results showing that certain experimentally observable quantum correlations cannot be reproduced by a Bell-local latent-variable model of the form

    P(A,B|a,b)
      = integral d lambda rho(lambda)
        P(A|a,lambda)P(B|b,lambda),

when the hidden variables lambda are sufficiently complete for the proposed common-cause explanation and are appropriately independent of the measurement settings a,b.

The theorem does not say that all hidden-variable theories are impossible. It does not say that faster-than-light signalling is possible. It does not say that determinism alone is false. Its content is more precise: the correlations of entangled systems violate constraints obeyed by the stated local causal model class.

1. The EPR-Bohm starting point

Prepare two spin-1/2 particles in the singlet state

    |psi^-> =
      (|up_z down_z> - |down_z up_z>)/sqrt(2).

Send one particle to Alice and the other to Bob. Alice chooses a unit vector a and measures

    A_hat = sigma·a,

while Bob chooses b and measures

    B_hat = sigma·b.

Outcomes are scaled to

    A,B in {-1,+1}.

For the singlet, quantum mechanics predicts

    E_QM(a,b)
      = <psi^-|
        (sigma·a) tensor (sigma·b)
        |psi^->
      = -a·b
      = -cos(theta_ab).

If a=b,

    E_QM(a,a)=-1,

so equal settings yield perfect anticorrelation.

The EPR question is whether the quantum state might be incomplete: perhaps each pair carries additional information lambda that determines, or at least probabilistically controls, the outcomes while preserving a local causal explanation.

2. What a Bell-local completion means

A deterministic local model assigns

    A=A(a,lambda),
    B=B(b,lambda),

with no dependence of Alice's response on Bob's setting and no dependence of Bob's response on Alice's setting.

A general stochastic Bell-local model uses

    P(A|a,lambda),
    P(B|b,lambda)

and assumes conditional factorization

    P(A,B|a,b,lambda)
      = P(A|a,lambda)P(B|b,lambda).

The observed distribution is then

    P(A,B|a,b)
      = integral d lambda rho(lambda)
        P(A|a,lambda)P(B|b,lambda).

The standard derivation also uses measurement independence:

    rho(lambda|a,b)=rho(lambda).

This means the distribution of the relevant source variables is not changed by which settings are selected.

These assumptions should be stated explicitly. The phrase "local realism" is historically common but is less precise because "realism" can mean many different things.

3. Why same-setting anticorrelation is not enough

Suppose Alice and Bob always use the same setting. A local source can simply emit an instruction table: for each possible direction, Alice receives a predetermined answer and Bob receives the opposite answer.

That reproduces perfect same-setting anticorrelation.

Therefore the decisive test must compare several alternative settings. The same hidden state lambda must provide mutually consistent local responses to all settings that could have been selected. Bell's insight is that these cross-setting consistency requirements impose observable inequalities.

4. Bell's original 1964-style inequality

Assume a deterministic local model reproduces perfect same-setting anticorrelation:

    B(n,lambda)=-A(n,lambda)

for every relevant n and almost every lambda.

Define

    E(a,b)
      = integral d lambda rho(lambda)
        A(a,lambda)B(b,lambda).

Using perfect anticorrelation,

    E(a,b)
      = - integral rho(lambda)
          A(a,lambda)A(b,lambda).

For three settings a,b,c,

    E(a,b)-E(a,c)
      = - integral rho A(a)
          [A(b)-A(c)].

Therefore

    |E(a,b)-E(a,c)|
      <= integral rho |A(b)-A(c)|.

For variables x,y in {-1,+1},

    |x-y|=1-xy.

Hence

    |E(a,b)-E(a,c)|
      <= 1 - integral rho A(b)A(c)
      = 1+E(b,c).

So every model satisfying these assumptions obeys

    |E(a,b)-E(a,c)| <= 1+E(b,c).

This is a Bell-1964-type inequality.

For the quantum singlet choose coplanar directions

    a=0°,
    b=60°,
    c=120°.

Quantum mechanics gives

    E(a,b)=-1/2,
    E(a,c)=+1/2,
    E(b,c)=-1/2.

The inequality would require

    1 <= 1/2,

which is false.

Bell's original argument therefore converted the EPR locality question into an experimentally distinguishable prediction.

5. Why CHSH was an important next step

The original three-setting derivation uses exact perfect anticorrelation. Real experiments never produce mathematical perfection.

Clauser, Horne, Shimony, and Holt introduced a four-setting inequality that does not require exact same-setting anticorrelation.

Give Alice settings a,a' and Bob settings b,b'. For fixed lambda define

    s(lambda)
      = A(a)B(b)
        +A(a)B(b')
        +A(a')B(b)
        -A(a')B(b').

Factor:

    s(lambda)
      = A(a)[B(b)+B(b')]
        +A(a')[B(b)-B(b')].

Because B(b),B(b') are each +/-1, one bracket is zero and the other is +/-2. Therefore

    s(lambda)=+/-2.

Averaging gives the CHSH parameter

    S=
      E(a,b)+E(a,b')
      +E(a',b)-E(a',b'),

with local bound

    |S|<=2.

6. Why stochastic local models obey CHSH too

Define conditional local means

    alpha_a(lambda)
      = sum_A A P(A|a,lambda),

    beta_b(lambda)
      = sum_B B P(B|b,lambda).

They lie in [-1,1].

Factorization gives

    E(a,b)
      = integral rho(lambda)
        alpha_a(lambda) beta_b(lambda).

For fixed lambda,

    s(lambda)
      = alpha_a(beta_b+beta_b')
        +alpha_a'(beta_b-beta_b').

Then

    |s(lambda)|
      <= |beta_b+beta_b'|
         +|beta_b-beta_b'|
      <=2.

Therefore

    |S|<=2.

Equivalently, every stochastic local strategy is a convex mixture of deterministic strategies, and a linear inequality valid at every deterministic vertex remains valid for every mixture.

Thus CHSH does not require fundamental determinism as a separate premise.

7. The full singlet probability distribution

For outcomes alpha,beta in {-1,+1},

    P(alpha,beta|a,b)
      = 1/4 [1-alpha beta (a·b)].

This formula immediately gives

    P(alpha|a,b)=1/2,
    P(beta|a,b)=1/2,

so the local marginals are independent of the remote setting.

The correlation is

    sum_alpha,beta
      alpha beta P(alpha,beta|a,b)
      = -a·b.

This distinction is central:
the singlet is operationally no-signalling, yet its joint correlations are not Bell-local.

8. The quantum CHSH violation

Choose coplanar settings

    a = 0°,
    a'=90°,
    b = 45°,
    b'=-45°.

Then

    E(a,b)   = -1/sqrt(2),
    E(a,b')  = -1/sqrt(2),
    E(a',b)  = -1/sqrt(2),
    E(a',b') = +1/sqrt(2).

Therefore

    S=-2sqrt(2),

and

    |S|=2sqrt(2)
       approximately 2.828427,

which exceeds the Bell-local limit 2.

9. Why the quantum maximum is 2sqrt(2)

For the singlet,

    S
      = -a·b-a·b'-a'·b+a'·b'
      = -a·(b+b')-a'·(b-b').

For fixed b,b', choose a and a' to align optimally. Then

    |S|
      <= |b+b'|+|b-b'|.

If phi is the angle between b and b',

    |b+b'|=2cos(phi/2),
    |b-b'|=2sin(phi/2).

Thus

    |S|
      <=2[cos(phi/2)+sin(phi/2)]
      <=2sqrt(2),

with equality at phi=90°.

A state-independent operator proof defines

    C=A tensor(B+B')
      +A' tensor(B-B').

For +/-1 observables,

    C^2=4I-[A,A'] tensor [B,B']

up to the equivalent sign convention. Because the commutator norms are at most 2,

    ||C||<=2sqrt(2).

This is Tsirelson's bound.

10. Three distinct correlation limits

For CHSH:

    Bell-local:      |S|<=2.
    Quantum:         |S|<=2sqrt(2).
    Algebraic:       |S|<=4.

The fact that quantum theory lies between the local and algebraic limits becomes even more revealing when no-signalling correlations are considered.

11. No-signalling is weaker than Bell locality

No-signalling requires only

    P(A|a,b)=P(A|a),
    P(B|a,b)=P(B|b).

Bell locality requires the stronger latent-variable decomposition

    P(A,B|a,b)
      = integral rho(lambda)
        P(A|a,lambda)P(B|b,lambda).

A hypothetical PR box makes the difference vivid. Let inputs x,y and outputs A_bit,B_bit be binary, with

    A_bit XOR B_bit = x*y,

while each local output is uniformly random.

The local marginals reveal nothing about the remote input, so the box is no-signalling. Yet it wins the CHSH game with probability 1 and reaches

    |S|=4.

Quantum mechanics is therefore more restrictive than no-signalling alone.

12. Why Bell violation does not enable faster-than-light communication

In the singlet experiment Alice cannot choose whether her result is +1 or -1. Her outcomes remain 50/50 no matter which setting Bob chooses.

Only after Alice and Bob later compare records through an ordinary communication channel do the correlations become visible.

Bell nonlocality means failure of a Bell-local common-cause factorization. It is not the same statement as operational superluminal signalling.

13. Counterfactual outcomes and incompatible observables

The deterministic CHSH derivation writes quantities such as

    A(a,lambda)
and
    A(a',lambda)

even though quantum mechanics may represent the corresponding observables by noncommuting operators.

This is not an assumption that quantum mechanics itself assigns simultaneous eigenvalues to incompatible measurements.

It is a property of the hidden-variable model being tested. Such a model is supposed to specify a local response for whichever setting is chosen. In a stochastic version it specifies a conditional distribution for each possible local input.

The four correlations are measured on four randomized subensembles, not simultaneously on one pair.

14. The local polytope

In the standard two-party, two-setting, two-outcome scenario, a deterministic local strategy specifies

    A0,A1,B0,B1 in {-1,+1}.

There are

    2^4=16

such strategies.

Every stochastic Bell-local behavior is a convex mixture of these 16 vertices.

Therefore the local set is a convex polytope.

A Bell inequality is a linear half-space constraint containing that polytope. Tight Bell inequalities correspond to facet boundaries.

This geometric viewpoint explains why Bell inequalities can be found and checked using linear programming.

15. Local-model membership as a linear program

Let v_k be the 16 deterministic local probability tables. Given an observed table P, ask whether weights w_k exist such that

    P=sum_k w_k v_k,
    w_k>=0,
    sum_k w_k=1.

This is a linear feasibility problem.

If it is feasible, the table has a local decomposition.

If it is infeasible, convex duality provides a separating linear functional: a Bell inequality violated by P.

For the ideal CHSH-optimal singlet table, the LP is infeasible.

For a noisy Werner state at the same settings,

    rho_v=v|psi^-><psi^-|+(1-v)I/4,

the correlation is

    E_v=-v a·b

and

    |S|=2sqrt(2)v.

At

    v=1/sqrt(2),

the behavior reaches the CHSH local boundary.

16. Fine's theorem

In the canonical 2x2x2 scenario, Fine's theorem connects several apparently different formulations.

Under the appropriate compatibility conditions, the following are equivalent:
- existence of a deterministic hidden-variable model;
- existence of a factorizable stochastic model;
- existence of one joint probability distribution for the four potential variables A0,A1,B0,B1 reproducing the accessible pairwise marginals;
- satisfaction of the complete relevant Bell/CHSH family.

This makes Bell violation a joint-distribution compatibility obstruction.

The theorem should not be generalized carelessly to arbitrary scenarios without checking its scope.

17. Clauser-Horne probability inequality

When detectors can fail, it is often better to work with event probabilities rather than correlations computed only on detected pairs.

For deterministic event indicators

    A1,A2,B1,B2 in {0,1},

define

    J=
      A1B1+A1B2+A2B1-A2B2-A1-B1.

Exhaustive enumeration gives

    J in {-1,0}.

Therefore after averaging,

    -1 <=
      P(A1B1)+P(A1B2)+P(A2B1)-P(A2B2)
      -P(A1)-P(B1)
      <=0.

This is a Clauser-Horne-type inequality.

Its experimental importance is that singles and nondetections can remain visible in the probability model instead of being silently removed.

18. The detection loophole

Suppose a detector clicks only on some trials, and click probability depends on the hidden variable and setting.

If one keeps only trials where both detectors fired, the effective hidden-variable distribution becomes

    rho(lambda | detected,a,b),

which can depend on a and b.

A local model can then make the detected sample look more strongly correlated than the full emitted ensemble.

Therefore a CHSH calculation performed only on joint detections is not automatically a loophole-free test.

One must either:
- explicitly assume fair sampling;
- achieve sufficient efficiency and include no-click events appropriately;
- or use a loss-aware Bell inequality such as a Clauser-Horne/Eberhard form.

19. Fair sampling

Fair sampling roughly asserts that the detected subset represents the full ensemble in a way that does not introduce setting-dependent hidden-variable bias relevant to the Bell statistic.

It can be a useful auxiliary assumption in some experiments, but a foundational Bell test ideally avoids depending on it.

High visibility among detected events does not by itself prove fair sampling.

20. The approximately 82.84% efficiency threshold

For the conventional symmetric two-party CHSH-style setting with a maximally entangled state and standard loss assumptions, the familiar critical detection efficiency is

    eta_crit = 2(sqrt(2)-1)
             approximately 0.828427.

This is not a universal Bell threshold.

It belongs to a specific state, inequality, symmetry assumption, and loss model.

21. Eberhard's 2/3 result

If the objective is not maximal ideal CHSH violation but minimal detector efficiency, a nonmaximally entangled state can perform better.

In the idealized symmetric, negligible-background regime, Eberhard-style optimization can lower the critical efficiency toward

    eta_crit=2/3
             approximately 66.67%.

As this limit is approached, the optimal state becomes weakly entangled and the absolute violation can become very small, making background counts increasingly important.

This illustrates a general research lesson:
"maximize ideal Bell violation" and "maximize robustness to loss" are different optimization problems.

22. Event-ready trials

An event-ready Bell test uses a heralding event to indicate that an entangled pair or remote entanglement event has successfully been established before the trial's measurement settings/outcomes are evaluated.

Advantages:
- cleaner trial definition;
- preparation failures need not be mistaken for detector losses;
- coincidence selection can be reduced.

The heralding event itself must still be included in the causal and statistical analysis.

23. The locality loophole

If information about Alice's setting can physically reach Bob before Bob's outcome is fixed, an ordinary communication strategy might mimic a Bell violation.

To exclude such explanations under relativistic causal assumptions, an experiment arranges relevant setting-choice and outcome events to be spacelike separated.

This requires:
- physical separation;
- fast setting generation;
- fast switching;
- characterized detector and electronics latency;
- synchronized clocks;
- conservative timing margins.

Distance alone is not enough.

24. The setting-independence or freedom-of-choice issue

The standard Bell model assumes

    rho(lambda|a,b)=rho(lambda).

Experiments support this assumption operationally by using physically independent random setting generators and choosing settings late relative to the source event.

Cosmic Bell tests use distant astronomical events to push possible ordinary common causes farther into the past.

No finite experiment can logically rule out every imaginable theory in which settings and source variables are correlated through unrestricted initial conditions. Such a theory rejects measurement independence rather than satisfying the standard Bell premises.

25. Biased settings

Bell settings do not have to be exactly 50/50 for every form of the theorem.

In the CHSH game, let the four input-pair probabilities be q_xy and assume they are independent of the hidden variable.

A deterministic local strategy must lose on at least one input pair, so it chooses to lose on the least probable pair. Therefore

    P_win <= 1-min_xy q_xy.

For uniform settings q_xy=1/4, this becomes

    P_win<=3/4.

Thus setting bias can be incorporated quantitatively rather than treated as a vague caveat.

26. Coincidence-time loophole

In continuous photonic experiments, detections are often paired if their timestamps fall within a coincidence window.

If detection timing depends on setting and hidden variables, the pairing rule itself may create setting-dependent postselection.

Safer approaches include:
- pulsed trials;
- externally clocked time bins;
- event-ready heralds;
- coincidence inequalities whose local bound accounts for the pairing rule.

27. Multipair emission and background

Photonic sources may emit more than one pair per trial. Multipair events can create accidental coincidences and reduce observed visibility.

Background and dark counts add detections unrelated to the intended pair.

These effects can interact with detector dead time, coincidence matching, and setting choices.

A stronger analysis treats them at the raw-trial level rather than subtracting favorable counts after the fact.

28. Detector dead time, afterpulsing, and channel mismatch

Detector dead time can make one trial depend on previous detections. Afterpulsing can generate temporally correlated spurious counts.

Different output channels may have different efficiencies.

Consequences:
- the data may not be i.i.d.;
- naive error formulas may fail;
- outcome frequencies can be biased.

A robust experiment either models these effects or uses statistical methods that remain valid under allowed history dependence.

29. Trial definition and postselection

A Bell theorem applies to a specified trial ensemble.

The experiment must predefine:
- when a trial begins;
- when it ends;
- settings;
- outcomes;
- no-click coding;
- double-click handling;
- invalid hardware states;
- inclusion and exclusion rules.

An outcome-dependent rule chosen after observing the data can invalidate the theorem-to-data mapping.

30. Why "several sigma above 2" can be insufficient

Suppose one estimates four correlations, combines them into S, and propagates Gaussian standard errors.

That may be adequate for an exploratory high-count i.i.d. analysis, but a foundational test faces a composite local null:
- devices can have memory;
- setting frequencies can vary;
- stopping can be adaptive;
- loss and trial selection matter;
- systematics may dominate.

A stronger analysis works at the per-trial level and proves a bound against the entire allowed local strategy class.

31. CHSH as a game

Let x,y be independent uniform input bits and let Alice and Bob output bits u,v.

They win if

    u XOR v = x*y.

A deterministic local strategy cannot satisfy all four input conditions. XORing the four required equations gives a contradiction.

Thus

    P_win^local <=3/4.

The optimal quantum strategy achieves

    P_win^quantum
      = cos^2(pi/8)
      = (2+sqrt(2))/4
      approximately 0.853553.

A PR box reaches 1.

32. Memory-robust statistics

Let W_i be the win indicator for trial i.

Under uniform independent inputs, even if a Bell-local device chooses its strategy from the entire previous history H_{i-1},

    E[W_i|H_{i-1}]<=3/4

provided the current settings satisfy the assumed independence.

Then

    W_i-3/4

has nonpositive conditional expectation under the local null.

The cumulative excess can be treated as a supermartingale, and concentration inequalities can bound how unlikely the observed excess is under all such history-dependent local strategies.

This avoids requiring identical independent trials.

33. Prediction-based ratios and e-values

Another approach constructs nonnegative per-trial factors R_i satisfying

    E_local[R_i|H_{i-1}]<=1

for every allowed local model.

Then

    T_n=product_i R_i

is a test supermartingale or e-process.

A large T_n provides evidence against the local null and can be compatible with optional stopping when the method is constructed correctly.

This framework can exploit the full outcome distribution rather than only S.

34. Optional stopping and multiple analysis choices

If an experimenter repeatedly checks an ordinary fixed-sample p-value and stops when it becomes small, the reported p-value is generally invalid.

Similarly, testing many:
- angle sets;
- time windows;
- inequalities;
- detector cuts;
and reporting only the strongest result inflates false-positive risk.

Solutions include:
- preregistration;
- fixed sample sizes;
- sequentially valid methods;
- multiplicity correction;
- held-out test data.

35. Effect size versus significance

These are different quantities.

Effect size:
    how far the observed behavior lies beyond a local boundary.

Significance:
    how incompatible the trial sequence is with the allowed local null after finite-sample uncertainty.

Systematic robustness:
    whether timing, detection, calibration, randomization, and data handling support the mathematical assumptions.

A complete experiment needs all three.

36. No-signalling diagnostics

One can separately test whether Alice's empirical marginal appears to vary with Bob's setting, and vice versa.

Apparent signalling can be caused by:
- finite-sample fluctuation;
- source drift;
- detector effects;
- coincidence artifacts;
- setting leakage.

A no-signalling fit can be useful diagnostically, but projecting raw data onto an exactly no-signalling model before the primary Bell test should not be done casually unless it is part of a prespecified valid analysis.

37. Bell's later local-causality language

Historically, Bell's 1964 theorem used deterministic hidden variables and a locality condition formulated in terms of the distant setting not affecting the local result.

Bell later developed a more explicitly probabilistic concept often called local causality or a theory of local beables, emphasizing screening-off by a sufficiently complete specification of relevant past variables.

Modern presentations often express this as factorization.

Keeping this historical distinction prevents later terminology from being projected backward as though it were Bell's original starting vocabulary.

38. Parameter independence and outcome independence

Factorization can be decomposed into conditions commonly called:

Parameter independence:

    P(A|a,b,lambda)=P(A|a,lambda),

and similarly for Bob.

Outcome independence:

    P(A|B,a,b,lambda)
      =P(A|a,b,lambda),

and similarly for Bob.

Together they yield factorization under ordinary conditions.

These terms are useful diagnostic decompositions, but one should be cautious about treating either one as the uniquely correct definition of physical locality.

39. The quantum set and the no-signalling set

In a fixed finite Bell scenario:

Local set:
a finite polytope generated by deterministic response strategies.

No-signalling set:
another polytope defined by positivity, normalization, and linear marginal-independence constraints.

Quantum set:
the convex set of probabilities

    P(a,b|x,y)
      =Tr[rho M_a^x tensor N_b^y].

The quantum set lies strictly between the other two in the CHSH scenario and is not simply another finite polytope.

40. NPA semidefinite hierarchy

For more complicated Bell scenarios, direct optimization over all states and measurement operators is difficult.

The Navascués-Pironio-Acín hierarchy constructs moment matrices of operator products and imposes positive-semidefinite consistency conditions.

Each level produces a semidefinite-program outer approximation to the relevant quantum correlation set.

It can be used to:
- upper-bound quantum Bell violations;
- test whether a candidate behavior is incompatible with a relaxation;
- generate numerical certificates.

A finite hierarchy level is generally an approximation, not automatically an exact characterization.

41. Bell inequalities beyond CHSH

CHSH is only the simplest nontrivial example.

Extensions include:
- chained inequalities with more settings;
- higher-outcome inequalities;
- multipartite Mermin-type inequalities;
- inequalities tailored to asymmetric loss;
- network Bell inequalities with multiple independent sources.

The universal research pattern is the same:
specify the causal model, derive its observable constraints, and compare them with quantum or experimental behaviors.

42. GHZ and Hardy

Later results showed that Bell nonlocality can also appear in forms not centered on a statistical inequality.

GHZ arguments use perfect multipartite parity predictions that are algebraically inconsistent with local predetermined values.

Hardy's paradox uses a pattern of zero-probability and positive-probability events that no local model can reproduce.

These are important later variants, not ingredients of Bell's original 1964 derivation.

43. Contextuality

Bell nonlocality is closely related to contextuality.

A Bell-local model requires Alice's response to her setting to be independent of which compatible remote measurement Bob performs.

General contextuality studies whether outcomes can be assigned consistently across measurement contexts even without spatial separation.

Bell scenarios add a particularly clear causal motivation for context independence through spacelike-separated choices.

44. Network nonlocality

Ordinary two-party Bell tests allow the two particles to share any common hidden variable lambda.

In network scenarios there may be multiple independent sources, for example

    rho(lambda_1,lambda_2)
      =rho_1(lambda_1)rho_2(lambda_2).

That extra source-independence condition changes the geometry and can produce nonlinear constraints such as bilocality inequalities.

Source independence therefore belongs to network Bell theory, not to the ordinary Bell theorem.

45. Self-testing

Near-maximal CHSH violation can strongly constrain the underlying quantum realization.

Under suitable assumptions, maximal CHSH violation implies, up to local isometries and irrelevant auxiliary systems, behavior equivalent to:
- a maximally entangled two-qubit state;
- approximately anticommuting local observables in the CHSH geometry.

Robust self-testing extends this to near-maximal violations.

46. Device-independent randomness

Bell violation can certify that outputs were not fully predetermined by Bell-local shared variables independent of the fresh inputs.

Quantitative protocols convert an observed violation into a lower bound on conditional min-entropy, account for finite-size effects and adversarial side information, and then apply a randomness extractor.

Bell violation is therefore not merely a philosophical result; it can become a cryptographic randomness resource.

47. Device-independent cryptography

In device-independent quantum key distribution, Alice and Bob use observed nonlocal correlations to bound an adversary's possible information without trusting detailed internal device models.

A real security proof must include:
- finite-size statistics;
- losses;
- input randomness;
- leakage during error correction;
- side information;
- composable security parameters.

A Bell violation by itself is not yet a full security proof.

48. Entanglement is not identical to Bell nonlocality

Every Bell-nonlocal quantum state is entangled.

But some entangled states do not violate a particular Bell inequality, and some mixed entangled states admit local models for broad measurement classes.

Therefore:

    Bell nonlocality => entanglement,

but entanglement alone does not guarantee an observed Bell violation in every scenario.

49. Bohmian mechanics

Bohmian mechanics is a hidden-variable theory that reproduces ordinary nonrelativistic quantum predictions.

Its dynamics for entangled systems is nonlocal in the Bell sense.

Therefore Bell's theorem does not eliminate hidden variables. It shows that hidden-variable theories reproducing quantum correlations cannot retain the tested Bell-local causal structure.

50. Retrocausal and measurement-dependent approaches

A retrocausal model can alter the ordinary forward-causal structure by allowing future settings to affect past variables.

A measurement-dependent or superdeterministic model allows correlations between lambda and the settings.

Such theories are not logically ruled out by a theorem whose premises they reject.

Their scientific evaluation then depends on whether they provide:
- a precise dynamical model;
- quantitative constraints;
- explanatory compression;
- additional testable consequences.

51. Everettian, collapse, and operational interpretations

Everettian approaches retain unitary dynamics and describe measurement records through branching.

Objective-collapse theories modify quantum dynamics.

Operational/Copenhagen-style approaches decline to posit Bell-local preexisting values for all alternative measurements.

All can reproduce ordinary Bell statistics in appropriate regimes, while telling different ontological stories.

Bell experiments constrain those stories but do not select one interpretation uniquely.

52. What Bell's theorem does not prove

It does not prove:
- controllable faster-than-light communication;
- impossibility of all hidden variables;
- falsity of determinism alone;
- a unique interpretation of quantum mechanics;
- that consciousness is required for measurement;
- that relativity's operational no-signalling structure has been experimentally overthrown;
- that the vague philosophical word "realism" by itself has been falsified.

It proves a precise incompatibility between observed/quantum correlations and a specified Bell-local causal model under stated auxiliary assumptions.

53. Landmark historical sequence

A compact chronology:

1935:
Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen argue that quantum mechanics may be incomplete under a locality-based reality criterion.

1951/1952:
Bohm reformulates EPR using spin and develops an explicit hidden-variable theory whose dynamics is nonlocal.

1964:
Bell derives an inequality showing that local hidden-variable completions cannot reproduce all quantum predictions.

1969:
Clauser, Horne, Shimony, and Holt formulate an experimentally practical four-setting inequality.

1972:
Freedman and Clauser perform an influential early photon test.

1974:
Clauser and Horne develop probability/rate formulations aimed at more realistic experiments.

1982:
Aspect, Dalibard, and Roger use rapidly varying analyzers.

1987/1993:
Garg-Mermin and Eberhard analyze detection-efficiency requirements and improved loss-tolerant strategies.

1998:
Weihs and collaborators implement fast random settings and strict spacelike-separation conditions in a photonic test.

2001:
Rowe and collaborators close the detection loophole with trapped ions, while locality remained open in that platform.

2015:
Hensen et al., Giustina et al., and Shalm et al. report experiments designed to close the principal detection and locality loopholes simultaneously using different physical platforms.

55. The complete logical chain

The argument can be compressed to:

A. Hypothesize a Bell-local common-cause model:
    P(A,B|a,b)
      = integral rho(lambda)
        P(A|a,lambda)P(B|b,lambda).

B. Assume the setting choices have the required independence from lambda.

C. For the 2x2x2 scenario, derive:
    |S|<=2.

D. Quantum mechanics predicts for the singlet:
    E(a,b)=-a·b.

E. At suitable angles:
    |S|=2sqrt(2)>2.

F. Experiments observe violations under increasingly stringent controls of loss, timing, randomization, trial definition, and finite statistics.

Therefore the full Bell-local latent-variable model class, with its stated auxiliary assumptions, cannot reproduce the observed correlation structure.

56. The deepest research lesson

The conceptual breakthrough is methodological.

Instead of asking:
"Can I invent a clever hidden-variable model that imitates these correlations?"

ask:
"What structural constraint is obeyed by every model in the entire causal class?"

That shift produces a theorem rather than an unsuccessful model search.

Then:
- test the theorem against quantum mechanics;
- use computation to find good settings;
- replace numerical conjectures with proof;
- rewrite the theorem in loss-aware observable form;
- design a spacetime-resolved randomized experiment;
- use finite-sample statistics valid against adaptive local devices;
- distinguish experimental evidence from interpretation.

Bell's theorem is therefore not only a result about quantum mechanics. It is a model example of how to turn a foundational disagreement into a falsifiable causal-inference problem.

57. A research-grade Bell experiment blueprint

A strong two-party Bell experiment can be described as the following protocol.

Preparation:
A source attempts to distribute an entangled state between Alice and Bob. If the architecture is event-ready, a herald establishes whether a valid Bell trial exists before settings are chosen.

Settings:
Alice and Bob choose settings using fast entropy sources. The setting probabilities and any known predictability bounds are logged.

Spacetime:
The setting-choice and outcome-registration events are arranged so that a signal constrained by the speed of light cannot carry the remote setting to the local outcome event in time.

Outcomes:
Every declared trial is assigned an outcome according to a rule fixed in advance. Nondetections and double detections are not silently discarded.

Data:
Store raw setting bits, raw detector events, timestamps, heralds, hardware-state flags, and trial IDs.

Analysis:
Compute a prespecified Bell statistic from the trial sequence.

Statistics:
Use a test whose null includes the allowed local memory, setting bias, and stopping rule.

Diagnostics:
Test setting balance, marginal no-signalling compatibility, detector rates, source drift, and timing stability separately.

Reproducibility:
Release enough raw data and code that an independent analyst can reconstruct the Bell statistic.

58. Assumption-to-hardware mapping

Bell factorization:
Supported experimentally by spacelike separation and the absence of known cross-wing communication channels.

Measurement independence:
Supported by independent setting generators, late setting choice, isolation, and quantified unpredictability.

Same source distribution across settings:
Supported by randomized interleaving rather than long setting blocks, plus source-stability diagnostics.

No postselection:
Supported by externally defined trials and explicit nondetection handling.

Valid finite-sample inference:
Supported by sequentially valid or prespecified fixed-sample statistics.

No hidden count manipulation:
Supported by raw-data retention, fixed event parsing, and independent software validation.

59. Detection efficiency numbers in context

Three frequently confused thresholds illustrate why context matters.

Visibility threshold for a Werner state at standard CHSH-optimal settings:

    v_crit=1/sqrt(2)
          approximately 70.71%.

This describes state/noise visibility, not detector efficiency.

Conventional symmetric maximally entangled CHSH detection threshold:

    eta_crit=2(sqrt(2)-1)
            approximately 82.84%

under the standard loss model.

Eberhard ideal symmetric threshold:

    eta_crit -> 2/3

with optimized nonmaximal entanglement and negligible background in the relevant probability formulation.

These numbers answer different questions.

60. Asymmetric detection

If one wing has nearly perfect detection, the required efficiency on the other wing can be substantially lower in appropriately optimized scenarios.

This is one reason atom-photon, matter-photon, and event-ready architectures are attractive.

Again, no single percentage should be quoted without the exact Bell scenario and loss model.

61. Source brightness is not simply "the higher the better"

Increasing source power can increase useful event rate but also:
- multipair emission;
- accidental coincidences;
- detector saturation;
- dead-time effects.

The best operating point maximizes statistical evidence per unit time after all these effects, not raw count rate alone.

62. Bell tests as causal inference

In modern causal language, the standard Bell DAG has a latent common cause lambda pointing to both outcomes and local settings pointing only to their local outcomes.

The observed Bell violation shows that this classical latent-variable DAG, with measurement independence and the specified screening-off relation, cannot generate the observed behavior.

One must change something:
- the causal structure;
- measurement independence;
- the probabilistic/ontological framework;
- or the idea that the outcomes can be represented by this local latent-variable decomposition.

This is why Bell theory is naturally connected to modern causal inference.

63. Why Bohmian mechanics matters historically

Bohmian mechanics existed before Bell and already demonstrated that hidden-variable theories were not ruled out in general.

Its dynamics is nonlocal for entangled systems.

That fact changes the historical question from:

"Are hidden variables possible?"

to:

"Can hidden variables reproduce quantum mechanics while preserving the relevant locality requirement?"

Bell's theorem answers the second question negatively.

64. Why earlier hidden-variable impossibility proofs were not enough

Earlier no-go arguments tried to exclude hidden-variable theories using assumptions about value assignments or expectation values.

Bell recognized that explicit hidden-variable theories existed and focused instead on locality.

This is one reason Bell's theorem had such impact: it tied an impossibility result to an experimentally accessible spacetime causal principle rather than merely to a formal representation assumption.

65. Bell and Kochen-Specker are related but different

Kochen-Specker contextuality rules out broad noncontextual value assignments.

Bell nonlocality uses separated parties and independently chosen settings.

A Bell test can therefore be viewed as a contextuality test with additional causal/spatial structure, but the two theorem families are not identical.

66. Modern optimization hierarchy

For a finite Bell scenario:

Local bound:
linear optimization over deterministic local vertices.

Quantum bound:
operator optimization; for many problems approximated by semidefinite programming such as NPA.

No-signalling bound:
linear optimization subject to positivity, normalization, and no-signalling equalities.

For CHSH this produces:

    2
    < 2sqrt(2)
    < 4.

This three-level hierarchy is one of the cleanest summaries of Bell theory.

67. Why numerical tools are scientifically useful

Enumeration:
checks every deterministic local strategy in a finite scenario.

Angle search:
locates candidate quantum optima.

Matrix eigensolvers:
verify spectra of concrete Bell operators.

Linear programming:
tests membership in the local polytope.

Semidefinite programming:
bounds quantum correlations in larger scenarios.

Monte Carlo:
tests expected finite-data behavior and analysis pipelines.

But every tool has a scope. A numerical optimizer suggesting 2.828427 is not a proof of 2sqrt(2); the analytic argument completes that step.

68. A concrete tool-validation example

For the standard CHSH geometry:

    a0=0°,
    a1=90°,
    b0=45°,
    b1=-45°,

the singlet correlations are numerically

    E00=-0.70710678,
    E01=-0.70710678,
    E10=-0.70710678,
    E11=+0.70710678.

Thus

    S=-2.82842712.

The corresponding CHSH Bell operator has extreme eigenvalues

    +/-2.82842712.

A local-polytope LP finds:
- ideal singlet table: infeasible;
- Werner v=0.70: feasible;
- v=1/sqrt(2): boundary;
- v=0.72: infeasible.

These are consistency checks linking algebra, quantum matrices, and convex geometry.

69. The status of 2015 experiments

In 2015, multiple groups reported Bell experiments designed to close the principal detection and locality loopholes simultaneously.

Hensen et al. used entangled electron spins separated by 1.3 km in an event-ready experiment.

Giustina et al. and Shalm et al. used high-efficiency entangled-photon systems.

The significance levels, architectures, and statistical methods differed, but together these experiments marked a major transition from tests requiring one major auxiliary loophole assumption to experiments addressing the standard principal loopholes within one protocol.

"Loophole-free" is useful shorthand, not a statement that empirical science has no assumptions.

70. Why no finite experiment eliminates unrestricted measurement dependence

A Bell test can choose settings using:
- quantum random sources;
- distant astronomical photons;
- independent laboratories;
- late decisions.

These steps constrain ordinary causal explanations linking source and settings.

But a theory that postulates correlations extending arbitrarily far into the common past or built into initial conditions rejects the standard measurement-independence assumption.

Bell data alone cannot logically force such a theory to accept that premise.

The meaningful scientific question is how much measurement dependence is required, what dynamics produces it, and whether the theory predicts anything else.

71. Why retrocausal models are not simply "loopholes"

A retrocausal theory changes the causal direction structure.

It may permit the future setting to affect variables in the source's past, thereby violating the standard Bell factorization or measurement-independence structure without ordinary faster-than-light influence.

This is a different theoretical framework, not an experimental loophole caused by bad detectors or timing.

That distinction—logical alternative versus laboratory loophole—is important.

72. The theorem/experiment/interpretation ledger

THEOREM:
Bell-local factorization plus measurement independence implies Bell inequalities.

THEOREM:
Quantum mechanics predicts violations for entangled states and suitable measurements.

THEOREM:
Quantum CHSH values are bounded by 2sqrt(2).

EMPIRICAL:
Bell experiments have repeatedly observed violations, including modern experiments closing the principal standard detection and locality loopholes under stated assumptions.

INTERPRETATION:
The observed world does not admit the tested local latent-variable explanation.

NOT A THEOREM:
One particular ontology must therefore be true.

73. The most compact rigorous statement

Let x,y be settings and a,b outcomes.

If

    P(a,b|x,y)
      = integral d lambda rho(lambda)
        P(a|x,lambda)P(b|y,lambda),

with

    rho(lambda|x,y)=rho(lambda),

then in the binary two-setting scenario the CHSH expression satisfies

    |S|<=2.

Quantum mechanics allows

    |S|=2sqrt(2),

and experiments realize correlations outside the local polytope.

That is Bell's theorem in operational mathematical form.

74. Why this result changed physics

Before Bell, one could reasonably imagine that quantum mechanics and a deeper local theory might make exactly the same empirical predictions.

Bell showed that locality is not an invisible philosophical decoration. It creates numerical constraints connecting mutually exclusive measurement choices.

Quantum mechanics violates those constraints.

That is the decisive conceptual move:
a debate about completeness became a laboratory test of causal structure.

75. Final distinction: Bell 1964 versus CHSH 1969

Bell 1964:
- closely tied to the EPR-Bohm perfect-correlation argument;
- uses perfect anticorrelation;
- yields a three-setting inequality;
- establishes the central impossibility result.

CHSH 1969:
- uses two settings for Alice and two for Bob;
- needs no exact perfect anticorrelation;
- yields the familiar
      |S|<=2
  inequality;
- is particularly convenient for experiments.

"Bell inequality" is now used generically for many local-model constraints, but historically Bell's original inequality and CHSH should not be conflated.

76. Final summary

A Bell-local hidden-variable model says that, after conditioning on a sufficiently complete common cause lambda, each wing responds only to its local setting, while lambda is appropriately independent of the setting choices.

That causal structure imposes observable consistency relations.

For CHSH:

    |S|<=2.

The singlet predicts:

    E(a,b)=-a·b,

and suitable directions give:

    |S|=2sqrt(2).

Quantum mechanics remains no-signalling, so the violation does not provide controllable faster-than-light communication.

Real experiments must connect the theorem to data without invalid postselection, with adequate detection, spacelike separation, independent setting choices, robust trial definitions, and finite-sample statistics that tolerate memory and stopping rules.

Modern Bell theory generalizes this result into convex geometry, semidefinite optimization, contextuality, network causality, self-testing, certified randomness, and device-independent cryptography.

Its central scientific lesson is broader than quantum foundations:

Define the explanatory model class precisely.
Derive a constraint that every model in that class must satisfy.
Search for a competing prediction outside the constraint.
Verify the result analytically and computationally.
Design the experiment so raw observations actually instantiate the theorem.
Audit every auxiliary assumption.
Only then interpret what has been ruled out.

11. FACTORIZATION OF THE SECOND-ORDER RELATIVISTIC OPERATOR
======================================================================

The first-order equation implies the second-order mass-shell equation.

for the free, time-independent H.

equivalent componentwise to the Klein-Gordon equation.

So the new equation does not contradict the relativistic quadratic relation; it factorizes it.

The obvious positive-energy choice,

    H = sqrt(c^2 p^2 + m^2 c^4),

becomes the spatially nonlocal operator

    sqrt(-ħ^2 c^2 ∇^2 + m^2 c^4)

in position space. It reproduces the energy but does not give the desired local first-order relativistic wave equation.

    {α_i,β} = 0,
    β^2 = I.

Why must the wavefunction have four components?

First, the dimension must be even. Since β^2=I, its eigenvalues are ±1. Because every α_i anticommutes with β and is invertible, α_i maps the β=+1 eigenspace bijectively onto the β=-1 eigenspace. The two eigenspaces therefore have equal dimension.

- derive the spin-statistics theorem;

THE DISCOVERED THEORY: FERMAT'S LAST THEOREM AND ITS PROOF ARCHITECTURE

1. The theorem

The investigation eventually discovers the statement now called Fermat's Last Theorem:

For every integer n>2, there are no positive integers x,y,z satisfying

    x^n+y^n=z^n.

The theorem contrasts sharply with n=2, where infinitely many Pythagorean triples exist.

Proof-depth labels used below:

[PROVED HERE]
Elementary reductions and the full exponent-4 descent.

[PROOF ARCHITECTURE EXPLAINED]
The structural mechanisms of the cubic/cyclotomic arguments and the modern modularity-lifting proof.

[IMPORTED DEEP THEOREM]
Results whose complete proofs are far larger than this training example, but whose exact role and hypotheses are identified.

2. Primitive reduction

The equation is homogeneous. Dividing a solution by gcd(x,y,z) produces a primitive one.

In a primitive solution the variables are pairwise coprime. If a prime divided two variables, the equation would force it to divide the third.

Thus a counterexample may always be assumed pairwise coprime.

3. Reduction of exponents

Suppose a solution exists for n>2.

If an odd prime p divides n, write n=pm:

    (x^m)^p+(y^m)^p=(z^m)^p.

If n has no odd prime divisor, then n is a power of 2 and, because n>2, is divisible by 4. Writing n=4m gives

    (x^m)^4+(y^m)^4=(z^m)^4.

Therefore it is enough to rule out:
- exponent 4;
- every odd prime exponent.

4. Why n=2 behaves differently

Every primitive Pythagorean triple with even first leg is

    X=2uv,
    Y=u^2-v^2,
    Z=u^2+v^2,

with u>v, gcd(u,v)=1 and opposite parity.

Geometrically, after dividing by Z^2 one obtains the conic

    U^2+V^2=1.

A rational line through one rational point parametrizes all rational points. Exponent 2 therefore has a genuine two-parameter solution mechanism.

5. Exponent 4: complete infinite descent

We prove the stronger claim

    x^4+y^4=w^2                                  (1)

has no positive solution.

Assume otherwise and choose a solution with minimal w. Divide out gcd(x,y). Fourth powers are 0 or 1 modulo 16, so exactly one of x,y is even; take x even.

Then

    (x^2)^2+(y^2)^2=w^2

is a primitive Pythagorean triple. Hence

    x^2=2mn,
    y^2=m^2-n^2,
    w=m^2+n^2,                                   (2)

where m>n, gcd(m,n)=1 and m,n have opposite parity.

Take m odd and n even. Write n=2n'. Then

    (x/2)^2=mn'.

Because gcd(m,n')=1 and mn' is a square,

    m=a^2,
    n'=b^2,
    n=2b^2.

Now

    y^2=a^4-4b^4,

so

    (2b^2)^2+y^2=(a^2)^2.                       (3)

This is another primitive Pythagorean triple:

    2b^2=2rs,
    y=r^2-s^2,
    a^2=r^2+s^2,

with gcd(r,s)=1. Hence b^2=rs, and coprimality forces

    r=c^2,
    s=d^2.

Therefore

    c^4+d^4=a^2.                                (4)

Equation (4) is another solution of the same type as (1), but with square-root variable a<w, contradicting minimality.

Thus x^4+y^4=w^2 has no positive solution, and therefore neither does

    x^4+y^4=z^4.

6. The cubic case and roots of unity

For n=3,

    x^3+y^3=(x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2).

The factors have gcd dividing 3. The exceptional prime prevents the naive conclusion that both factors are cubes.

Introduce a primitive cube root of unity ω. In the Eisenstein integers Z[ω],

    x^3+y^3=(x+y)(x+ωy)(x+ω^2y).

The norm

    N(a+bω)=a^2-ab+b^2

is Euclidean, so the ring is a UFD. The prime 3 ramifies:

    3=unit·(1-ω)^2.

A cubic descent tracks the unique exceptional prime above 3. After removing the forced ramified factor, the remaining coprime factors must be cubes up to units. Comparing coefficients in a cube produces a strictly smaller primitive cubic solution. Infinite descent rules out

    x^3+y^3=z^3.

This special case reveals the general strategy:
split the polynomial completely, track ramified primes, use factorization, and descend.

7. General prime exponent and the cyclotomic program

For odd prime p, let ζ_p be a primitive pth root of unity:

    x^p+y^p=∏_{k=0}^{p-1}(x+ζ_p^k y).

The natural ring is Z[ζ_p]. The rational prime p is highly ramified:

    p=unit·(1-ζ_p)^{p-1}.

The tempting proof would make the linear factors into pth powers. That requires factorization control.

But rings of algebraic integers need not be UFDs.

The repair is ideal theory: every nonzero ideal in the ring of integers of a number field has unique prime-ideal factorization.

A second obstruction remains. If

    I^p=(α),

the ideal I need not be principal. Its ideal class may be nontrivial p-torsion.

This is the exact class-group obstruction to the naive generalized factorization proof.

8. Regular primes and Kummer's theorem

An odd prime p is called regular when p does not divide the class number of Q(ζ_p).

Kummer's criterion relates this to Bernoulli numbers: p is regular exactly when it divides none of the relevant numerators

    B_2,B_4,...,B_{p-3}.

Kummer proved Fermat's Last Theorem for every regular prime exponent.

The first irregular primes are 37,59,67. Thus the cyclotomic program solves a huge family but not every prime.

Regularity must not be confused with class number 1. The relevant condition is absence of the p-primary class-group obstruction.

9. Classical local refinements

Prime exponents split into the classical first and second cases according to whether p divides xyz.

Auxiliary-prime arguments and later congruence criteria impose very strong necessary conditions on a hypothetical solution. They eliminate many exponents and expose arithmetic structure, but a finite family of congruence checks cannot prove a universal theorem over infinitely many prime exponents.

10. Geometric reformulation

The equation defines the projective curve

    C_n:X^n+Y^n=Z^n.

A smooth plane curve of degree n has genus

    g=(n-1)(n-2)/2.

Therefore:
- n=2 has genus 0;
- n=3 has genus 1;
- n≥4 has genus >1.

Faltings's theorem says a genus>1 curve over Q has only finitely many rational points.

That does not prove Fermat's Last Theorem: finite is not the same as empty.

The modern proof attaches a different curve to a hypothetical solution.

11. The Frey curve

Let p≥5 and suppose

    a^p+b^p=c^p                               (5)

is a primitive solution.

Set A=a^p and B=b^p and define

    E:y^2=x(x-A)(x+B).                        (6)

The cubic roots are 0,A,-B; their pairwise differences are A,B,A+B=c^p.

For the Weierstrass model

    y^2=x^3+(B-A)x^2-ABx,

one computes

    c4=16(A^2+AB+B^2),

and

    Δ=16A^2B^2(A+B)^2
     =16(abc)^{2p}.                            (7)

At every odd q|abc, q divides Δ but not c4, so the reduction is multiplicative. The discriminant valuation at each such q is a multiple of p.

After the standard normalization at 2, the curve is semistable.

This is the Frey curve.

12. The residual Galois representation

The p-torsion points form

    E[p]≅(Z/pZ)^2.

The absolute Galois group acts:

    ρ̄_{E,p}:G_Q→GL_2(F_p).

At a prime q of good reduction,

    a_q(E)=q+1-#E(F_q),

and Frobenius has characteristic polynomial

    T^2-a_q(E)T+q.

Thus the representation packages local point-count data at infinitely many primes.

The representation must be irreducible for level lowering. Reducibility would give a rational p-isogeny. The required irreducibility for the Frey situation is a genuine imported theorem from rational-isogeny/Frey-curve arithmetic; it is not automatic for every elliptic curve.

13. Modular forms and modular elliptic curves

A normalized weight-2 cuspidal Hecke eigenform has

    f(q)=Σ_{n≥1}a_nq^n.

Deep theory attaches two-dimensional Galois representations to such forms with Frobenius traces a_q.

An elliptic curve over Q is modular when its arithmetic data agree with those of an appropriate weight-2 newform.

This creates the bridge

    elliptic curves ↔ Galois representations ↔ modular forms.

14. Ribet's level lowering

Assume the Frey curve is modular.

Then its mod-p representation is modular. Because of the special local behavior forced by (7), Ribet's level-lowering theorem removes the odd primes dividing abc from the residual modular level, after checking irreducibility and the local hypotheses.

The primes 2 and p require separate local arguments.

The final residual representation would have to come from a nonzero weight-2 cusp form of level 2.

But

    S_2(Γ_0(2))=0.

Indeed X_0(2) has genus 0, while weight-2 cusp forms correspond to holomorphic differentials.

Therefore the Frey curve attached to a hypothetical solution cannot be modular.

Important distinction:
the original elliptic curve does not acquire conductor 2. Level lowering concerns a lower-level modular realization of its residual representation.

15. The remaining target: semistable modularity

The Diophantine problem is now reduced to:

    Every semistable elliptic curve over Q is modular.             (SM)

If SM holds, the Frey curve would be modular because it is semistable, and nonmodular because of level lowering. Contradiction.

16. Residual modularity and lifting

For a small prime ℓ, the curve gives

    ρ:G_Q→GL_2(Z_ℓ)

and residual representation

    ρ̄:G_Q→GL_2(F_ℓ).

The strategy is:
1. prove ρ̄ modular;
2. prove any lift satisfying the correct local conditions is modular;
3. verify ρ is such a lift.

Step 2 is modularity lifting.

17. Universal deformation ring R

Fix an absolutely irreducible ρ̄ and prescribe local/global deformation conditions.

For every suitable complete local coefficient ring A, consider lifts

    ρ_A:G_Q→GL_2(A)

satisfying those conditions.

Deformation theory constructs a universal ring R so that maps R→A correspond to allowed lifts.

R parameterizes all permitted Galois deformations.

18. Hecke algebra T

On the modular side, localize the Hecke algebra acting on the relevant modular forms at the maximal ideal corresponding to ρ̄.

Call it T.

The modular Galois representation valued in T satisfies the same deformation conditions, giving a natural surjection

    R→T.

Surjectivity does not prove every lift is modular.

The key target is

    R≅T.                                         (8)

If R=T, every allowed deformation is modular.

19. Selmer groups and obstruction theory

First-order deformations are controlled by Galois cohomology of

    ad^0(ρ̄).

The local conditions define a Selmer group. Dual local conditions define a dual Selmer group measuring the obstruction/excess deformation directions.

This is why a superficial dimension count cannot prove R=T.

20. Taylor–Wiles auxiliary primes

Choose auxiliary primes q with conditions such as

    q≡1 mod ℓ^N

and suitable residual Frobenius eigenvalues.

They are chosen to kill dual Selmer classes through their local conditions.

Simultaneously they create large ℓ-power diamond-operator groups on the modular side.

For carefully selected sets Q_N one obtains:
- deformation rings R_{Q_N};
- Hecke algebras T_{Q_N};
- modules M_{Q_N} carrying both actions.

21. Patching and the numerical criterion

As N grows, patch compatible finite-level modules into a limiting module M_∞ over a power-series-type ring S_∞ and a patched deformation ring R_∞.

The auxiliary variables and symmetry force strong depth and freeness properties.

Commutative algebra then compares dimensions, depths, generators, relations, cotangent data, and modular congruence data.

The Wiles numerical criterion and the Taylor–Wiles patching argument force the Galois and modular parameter spaces to coincide.

Descending from the patched system gives the minimal R=T theorem; further arguments handle the relevant nonminimal conditions.

This is the content behind the slogan

    R=T.

22. Residual modularity at 3

If E[3] is irreducible, its projective image lies in

    PGL_2(F_3)≅S_4,

which is solvable.

The Langlands–Tunnell theorem supplies residual modularity. The 3-adic lifting theorem then shows E is modular.

23. The 3–5 trick

If E[3] is reducible, rational-isogeny analysis in the semistable setting forces E[5] to be irreducible.

Construct another elliptic curve A satisfying

    A[5]≅E[5]

while A[3] is irreducible.

Then

    A[3] modular
      ⇒ A modular
      ⇒ A[5] modular
      ⇒ E[5] modular
      ⇒ E modular.

This is the 3–5 trick.

Thus every semistable elliptic curve over Q is modular.

24. Historical proof and repair

The semistable modularity theorem was proved by Andrew Wiles, with a crucial ring-theoretic repair developed with Richard Taylor.

The corrected papers appeared in 1995:

Andrew Wiles,
"Modular elliptic curves and Fermat's Last Theorem,"
Annals of Mathematics 141 (1995), 443–551.

Richard Taylor and Andrew Wiles,
"Ring-theoretic properties of certain Hecke algebras,"
Annals of Mathematics 141 (1995), 553–572.

The level-lowering theorem used in the Fermat implication is associated with Kenneth Ribet's 1990 work on modular Galois representations.

25. Complete logical chain

A. Any counterexample for n>2 produces one for n=4 or an odd prime p.

B. n=4 is impossible by the complete infinite descent.

C. p=3 is impossible by cubic descent in the Eisenstein integers.

D. Let p≥5 and suppose

       a^p+b^p=c^p.

E. Build

       E:y^2=x(x-a^p)(x+b^p).

F. E is semistable and its mod-p representation is irreducible.

G. If E is modular, Ribet's level lowering forces a nonzero element of

       S_2(Γ_0(2)).

H. But

       S_2(Γ_0(2))=0.

   Therefore E is nonmodular.

I. Wiles/Taylor–Wiles semistable modularity says E is modular.

J. Contradiction.

Therefore no p≥5 solution exists.

Together with p=3, n=4, and exponent reduction, no positive solution exists for any n>2.

26. What computation can and cannot do

Computation can:
- search bounded triples;
- enumerate power residues;
- test local obstructions;
- verify algebraic identities;
- compute c4 and discriminants;
- inspect Bernoulli numerators in finite ranges;
- count points on elliptic curves modulo primes;
- compute finite-dimensional modular-form spaces.

No finite search proves the theorem. The theorem quantifies over infinitely many triples and exponents.

The proof succeeds by changing representation until a hypothetical solution forces an object that two independent theories classify incompatibly.

27. Research methodology

The discovery path is a sequence of justified abstractions:

1. normalize;
2. experiment;
3. explain the positive control;
4. reduce the parameter family;
5. use congruences as filters;
6. exploit descent when self-similarity appears;
7. enlarge the number system when a polynomial refuses to split;
8. replace element factorization by ideal factorization when UFD fails;
9. identify the class-group obstruction;
10. move to geometry when the algebraic route becomes nonuniform;
11. design an auxiliary curve from the discriminant one wants;
12. reduce its arithmetic modulo the original exponent;
13. compare its Galois data with a second global theory;
14. lower the residual level to an impossible endpoint;
15. prove modularity by comparing all allowed Galois lifts with modular lifts;
16. kill obstruction groups using auxiliary primes;
17. patch and prove R=T;
18. bootstrap residual modularity through the 3–5 trick.

The final contradiction is short:

    hypothetical Fermat solution
      ⇒ semistable Frey curve
      ⇒ nonmodular by level lowering,

while independently

    semistable elliptic curve
      ⇒ modular by Wiles/Taylor–Wiles.

The same curve cannot be both.

That completes the theorem.
