PHASE 91 — CHANNEL RESOLVABILITY
======================================================================

Channel resolvability asks:
How much randomness/rate is required so that channel outputs induced by a random codebook approximate a target output distribution?

It is deeply connected to:
- secrecy;
- soft covering;
- simulation;
- random coding.

This is a more advanced operational role of mutual information:
not only reliable transmission, but approximation of output statistics.

======================================================================
PHASE 92 — RANDOMNESS EXTRACTION
======================================================================

A biased or partially predictable source may contain less usable uniform randomness than its alphabet size suggests.

For independent repeated sources, Shannon entropy controls average compressibility, but cryptographic extraction often depends on min-entropy or smooth min-entropy.

This reinforces the rule:
choose the entropy notion according to the operational task.

======================================================================
PHASE 93 — STRONG DATA PROCESSING
======================================================================

Ordinary data processing says:

    I(U;Y)<=I(U;X)

for U->X->Y.

A strong data-processing inequality seeks a contraction factor eta<1:

    I(U;Y)<=eta I(U;X)

for a fixed noisy channel under appropriate conditions.

This quantifies not merely that information decreases, but how much a channel contracts dependence.

Applications include:
- distributed inference;
- mixing;
- lower bounds;
- privacy.

======================================================================
PHASE 94 — COMMON INFORMATION AND COORDINATION
======================================================================

Two terminals may wish to generate correlated actions rather than transmit a message.

Questions of common randomness and common information ask:
How many shared bits are needed to synthesize a joint distribution?

This is a different operational problem from compression, despite using the same mutual-information toolbox.

Research significance:
Information quantities derive meaning from tasks. The same joint law can support multiple inequivalent operational rates.

======================================================================
PHASE 95 — CAUSAL INFORMATION FLOW
======================================================================

Ordinary mutual information is symmetric and does not encode direction of time.

For sequential systems with feedback, define directed information:

    I(X^n -> Y^n)
    =
    sum_{t=1}^n
      I(X^t;Y_t | Y^{t-1}).

This respects causal ordering.

Use cases:
- feedback channels;
- control;
- causal inference-like communication models.

Important:
Directed information is not needed for an ordinary memoryless channel without feedback. Introduce it only when the causal architecture demands it.

======================================================================
PHASE 96 — NETWORK CUT-SET THINKING
======================================================================

In a communication network, any cut separating sources from destinations imposes an information-flow bottleneck.

A generic cut-set converse says that rates crossing a cut cannot exceed mutual information across that cut under allowable input distributions.

This generalizes the point-to-point converse concept:
capacity is constrained by every information bottleneck.

Network achievability can be much harder than cut-set upper bounds.

======================================================================
PHASE 97 — WHY SOME NETWORK PROBLEMS REMAIN OPEN
======================================================================

For a point-to-point memoryless channel, one scalar optimization solves capacity.

For interference networks:
- each transmitter both helps its receiver and harms others;
- decoding strategies may treat interference as noise, decode it, split messages, or align signals;
- simple single-letter regions may be insufficient.

A research-grade theory should not imply that one formula solves all networks.

The existence of open capacity-region problems is itself an important lesson:
foundational quantities can be complete while complex architectures remain mathematically unresolved.

======================================================================
PHASE 98 — GENERAL SOURCES AND CHANNELS
======================================================================

Suppose source law changes with n or is nonergodic.

The quantity:

    -(1/n)log P_{X^n}(X^n)

may fail to converge to a constant.

Similarly:

    (1/n)i(X^n;Y^n)

may have multiple limiting behaviors.

Information-spectrum theory uses probabilistic limsup/liminf quantities rather than assuming a single entropy or mutual-information rate.

This turns classical iid theorems into corollaries of broader general-source/channel results.

======================================================================
PHASE 99 — ADVERSARIAL CHANNELS
======================================================================

Random noise and adversarial errors are different models.

If an adversary can choose corruptions subject to constraints, Shannon's stochastic channel formulas need not apply directly.

Coding theory then studies:
- minimum distance;
- worst-case error correction;
- arbitrarily varying channels;
- symmetrizability;
- list decoding.

Research warning:
"10% error probability" and "up to 10% adversarial errors" are not interchangeable statements.

======================================================================
PHASE 100 — COMPUTATIONAL COMPLEXITY
======================================================================

Information theory often proves existence of optimal or near-optimal codes without efficient algorithms.

Random coding plus maximum-likelihood decoding can be computationally infeasible.

Modern coding theory asks for:
- near-capacity rates;
- low decoding complexity;
- finite length;
- manageable latency;
- robustness.

Examples include LDPC, turbo, and polar coding families.

The information-theoretic limit is a benchmark, not an implementation recipe.

======================================================================
PHASE 101 — SEMANTIC/TASK-ORIENTED EXTENSION
======================================================================

If the receiver need not reconstruct raw data, source fidelity should be defined by task loss.

Examples:
- classify an object;
- estimate a parameter;
- trigger a control action.

Then a bit that changes the decision can matter more than many bits that do not.

Classical rate-distortion already provides a formal doorway:
choose distortion d(x,xhat) to reflect task value.

But designing a semantically faithful distortion is itself a modeling problem and may require domain knowledge outside classical information theory.

======================================================================
PHASE 102 — RESEARCH PRACTICE: INVARIANCE CHECKS
======================================================================

When proposing an information quantity, test:

Relabeling:
Does arbitrary renaming of symbols change it?

Product composition:
How does it behave for independent systems?

Coarse-graining:
Does processing obey a monotonicity law?

Units:
How does log base change the quantity?

Coordinate transformation:
For continuous variables, is the claimed meaning invariant?

Operational interpretation:
Can a code, test, estimator, or decision problem realize it?

Boundary cases:
What happens at deterministic laws, disjoint supports, zero noise, complete noise, zero distortion, or infinite precision?

This checklist catches many false definitions before deep proof work begins.

======================================================================
PHASE 103 — RESEARCH PRACTICE: ACHIEVABILITY/CONVERSE PAIRING
======================================================================

A fundamental limit is incomplete until both sides are understood.

Achievability asks:
Can a construction attain the proposed rate?

Converse asks:
Can anything beat it?

Examples:

Source coding:
- achievability: typical-set indexing or arithmetic coding;
- converse: counting/Kraft/information inequalities.

Channel coding:
- achievability: random coding;
- converse: Fano + data processing + single-letterization.

Rate-distortion:
- achievability: random covering;
- converse: mutual-information lower bound.

Slepian-Wolf:
- achievability: random binning;
- converse: conditional entropy + Fano.

This paired architecture is one of the most transferable lessons in theoretical research.

======================================================================
PHASE 104 — RESEARCH PRACTICE: FIRST-, SECOND-, AND ERROR-EXPONENT ORDERS
======================================================================

For any asymptotic theorem, ask three questions:

First order:
What is the limiting rate?
Examples H, C, R(D).

Second order:
How far from the limit at finite n?
Examples varentropy, channel dispersion, rate-distortion dispersion.

Exponent:
How quickly does failure probability decay when operating away from the boundary?
Examples source reliability, channel error exponents, large-deviation rates.

This hierarchy prevents "capacity" from being mistaken for a complete engineering prediction.

======================================================================
PHASE 105 — RESEARCH PRACTICE: MODEL MISSPECIFICATION
======================================================================

Theorems assume a model.

If actual distribution is P but designer assumes Q:
- compression suffers redundancy;
- a decoder may be mismatched;
- claimed error exponents can fail;
- capacity-achieving inputs may change.

Robust information theory asks performance over uncertainty classes.

Universal coding is one response on the source side.
Compound channels and arbitrarily varying channels are responses on the channel side.

A research-grade agent should ask:
"Which theorem survives if the assumed law is slightly wrong?"

======================================================================
PHASE 106 — RESEARCH PRACTICE: NONASYMPTOTIC CHECK BEFORE LIMIT
======================================================================

Before trusting an asymptotic theorem, calculate a small finite case.

Examples:
- exact Huffman length vs H;
- exact binomial type count vs 2^{nH};
- simulated random-code error at finite n;
- normal approximation vs C;
- finite distortion codebook cardinality.

This exposes:
- integer constraints;
- polynomial factors;
- boundary effects;
- slow convergence.

Asymptotics explain structure, but finite examples protect against misuse.

======================================================================
PHASE 107 — FINAL RESEARCH FRONTIER MAP
======================================================================

Classical core:
- entropy/divergence/mutual information;
- source coding;
- channel coding;
- rate-distortion.

Deep extensions:
- universal coding;
- hypothesis testing and large deviations;
- finite blocklength;
- distributed source coding;
- multi-user channels;
- feedback;
- secrecy;
- coordination;
- information spectrum;
- network information theory.

Adjacent theories:
- coding theory under adversarial errors;
- algorithmic information;
- statistical decision theory;
- estimation theory;
- learning theory;
- control;
- quantum information.

Open-ended frontier:
No single scalar notion of "information" solves every task. The mature lesson is to derive the right operational quantity from the problem rather than treating entropy as a universal magic number.

PHASE 108 — POST-DISCOVERY LITERATURE CROSS-CHECK
======================================================================

This phase is intentionally delayed until after the independent derivation.

A. FOUNDATIONAL MATCH.
Shannon's 1948 paper frames the communication problem as reproducing a selected message exactly or approximately and explicitly separates the engineering problem from semantic meaning. It develops a logarithmic uncertainty measure, source coding ideas, noisy-channel capacity, and the possibility of reliable communication below a critical rate.

FINAL THEORY — INFORMATION THEORY FROM FOUNDATIONS TO RESEARCH-LEVEL STRUCTURE

1. SCOPE

Information theory is a mathematical theory of the limits of representation, compression, inference, and communication under uncertainty.

Its foundational quantities are probabilistic rather than semantic. The theory asks questions such as:

- How unpredictable is a random source?
- How many bits are required to represent it?
- How much can one observation reveal about another?
- How many reliable messages can pass through a noisy channel?
- How much rate is required if approximation is allowed?
- How do these limits change with side information, memory, finite blocklength, or multiple users?

The answers depend on the operational criterion. "How many bits are needed?" has different answers for variable-length exact coding, fixed-length coding with vanishing error, fixed-length zero-error coding, and lossy coding.

Unless otherwise stated, logarithms are base 2 and units are bits.

======================================================================
2. SELF-INFORMATION
======================================================================

For outcome x with probability p(x), define self-information or surprisal:

    i(x)=-log2 p(x).

Why logarithmic?

Independent events have multiplying probabilities:
    p(x,y)=p(x)p(y).

A sensible additive information measure should satisfy:
    i(x,y)=i(x)+i(y).

The logarithm is the regular solution to this composition requirement.

Examples:

    p=1       -> 0 bits
    p=1/2     -> 1 bit
    p=1/8     -> 3 bits
    p=0.01    -> 6.643856 bits

Self-information describes the realized outcome. To characterize the source before observing it, average over outcomes.

======================================================================
3. SHANNON ENTROPY
======================================================================

For discrete X:

    H(X)
    =E[-log2 p(X)]
    =-sum_x p(x)log2 p(x).

Basic properties:

    H(X)>=0.

If X is deterministic:
    H(X)=0.

If X has at most N possible values:
    H(X)<=log2 N,

with equality for the uniform distribution.

For Bernoulli(p):

    h2(p)
    =-p log2 p-(1-p)log2(1-p).

Examples:

    h2(1/2)=1.
    h2(0.1)=0.4689955936.

Entropy has several mutually reinforcing interpretations:

1. expected surprise;
2. logarithmic effective number of likely long sequences;
3. asymptotic lossless compression rate under standard criteria;
4. uncertainty before observation.

Axiomatic characterizations based on continuity, symmetry, and grouping/recursion select this functional form up to choice of logarithm base.

======================================================================
4. CONCAVITY AND MAXIMUM ENTROPY
======================================================================

Entropy is concave in the probability distribution.

For distributions p_j and mixture weights lambda_j:

    H(sum_j lambda_j p_j)
    >=sum_j lambda_j H(p_j).

This expresses that unresolved mixing adds uncertainty.

The uniform distribution maximizes entropy on a finite support:

    H(p)<=log2 N.

Maximum-entropy reasoning extends to continuous problems, but differential entropy requires additional caution.

======================================================================
5. JOINT AND CONDITIONAL ENTROPY
======================================================================

Joint entropy:

    H(X,Y)
    =-sum_{x,y}p(x,y)log2 p(x,y).

Conditional entropy:

    H(Y|X)
    =-sum_{x,y}p(x,y)log2 p(y|x).

Chain rule:

    H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y|X).

Equivalently:

    H(X,Y)=H(Y)+H(X|Y).

For many variables:

    H(X_1,...,X_n)
    =sum_i H(X_i|X_1,...,X_{i-1}).

For discrete variables:

    H(X|Y)<=H(X).

The difference is mutual information.

======================================================================
6. RELATIVE ENTROPY / KL DIVERGENCE
======================================================================

For distributions p and q:

    D(p||q)
    =sum_x p(x)log2[p(x)/q(x)].

If p(x)>0 and q(x)=0 for any x, then:

    D(p||q)=+infinity.

Properties:

    D(p||q)>=0,

with equality iff p=q almost everywhere with respect to p.

KL divergence is not generally symmetric:

    D(p||q) != D(q||p).

It is not a metric.

Operational interpretations include:

- excess logarithmic prediction loss;
- excess ideal coding cost under model mismatch;
- expected log-likelihood ratio;
- asymptotic evidence rate in hypothesis testing;
- rare-event exponent in large deviations.

======================================================================
7. CROSS-ENTROPY
======================================================================

Cross-entropy:

    H(p,q)
    =-sum_x p(x)log2 q(x).

Identity:

    H(p,q)=H(p)+D(p||q).

Therefore predicting q when truth is p incurs an excess expected log loss equal to D(p||q).

Because D>=0, expected log loss is minimized by using the true distribution.

======================================================================
8. MUTUAL INFORMATION
======================================================================

Mutual information:

    I(X;Y)
    =H(X)-H(X|Y).

Equivalent forms:

    I(X;Y)
    =H(Y)-H(Y|X)
    =H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y).

Most importantly:

    I(X;Y)
    =D(p_XY || p_X p_Y).

Consequences:

    I(X;Y)>=0.

And:

    I(X;Y)=0
    iff X and Y are independent.

Mutual information detects arbitrary statistical dependence, not only linear correlation.

Conditional mutual information:

    I(X;Y|Z)
    =H(X|Z)-H(X|Y,Z).

Chain rule:

    I(X;Y,Z)
    =I(X;Y)+I(X;Z|Y).

======================================================================
9. INFORMATION DENSITY
======================================================================

The pointwise information density is

    i(x;y)
    =log2[p(y|x)/p(y)].

Its expectation is mutual information:

    E[i(X;Y)]=I(X;Y).

For blocks:

    i(x^n;y^n)
    =log2[p(y^n|x^n)/p(y^n)].

Information density is central in:

- finite-blocklength coding;
- hypothesis testing;
- information-spectrum methods;
- concentration arguments.

Mutual information is the first-order average; the distribution of information density contains finer operational information.

======================================================================
10. DATA PROCESSING
======================================================================

If:

    X -> Y -> Z

is a Markov chain, then:

    I(X;Z)<=I(X;Y).

This is the data-processing inequality.

Interpretation:
A transformation of Y cannot create additional information about X that was absent from Y.

Equality relates to sufficiency: Z may preserve all Y-information relevant to X even while discarding irrelevant details.

Important nuance:
A processor can increase the entropy of its output by adding noise. Data processing says it cannot increase information about the upstream variable.

======================================================================
11. FANO'S INEQUALITY
======================================================================

Let W take M possible values and let W_hat be an estimate from observation Y. If:

    P_e=P[W_hat != W],

then:

    H(W|Y)
    <=h2(P_e)+P_e log2(M-1).

Fano's inequality translates uncertainty into a decoding-error constraint.

It is a standard converse tool: reliable estimation of one of many possibilities requires the observation to carry almost all of the message uncertainty.

======================================================================
12. METHOD OF TYPES
======================================================================

For a length-n sequence over an m-symbol alphabet, its type is its empirical distribution.

Number of possible types:

    <=(n+1)^m.

For type q:

    |T(q)|
    approximately 2^{nH(q)}

up to polynomial factors.

A useful bound is:

    (n+1)^(-m) 2^{nH(q)}
    <=|T(q)|
    <=2^{nH(q)}.

If the true iid law is p, a type q has probability approximately:

    2^{-nD(q||p)}

up to subexponential factors.

This connects entropy to counting and KL divergence to rare empirical laws.

======================================================================
13. ASYMPTOTIC EQUIPARTITION PROPERTY
======================================================================

For iid discrete X_i:

    -(1/n)log2 p(X^n)
    ->H(X)

in probability.

For large n, most mass lies in a typical set containing roughly:

    2^{nH(X)}

sequences, each with probability roughly:

    2^{-nH(X)}.

Weak typicality:
defined through normalized log probability.

Strong typicality:
defined through empirical frequencies and most useful for finite alphabets.

Joint typicality:
a pair (x^n,y^n) has empirical/joint likelihood behavior close to p_XY.

Conditional typicality:
given a typical x^n, channel-generated y^n is overwhelmingly likely to have the appropriate conditional empirical behavior.

These distinctions matter in rigorous coding proofs.

======================================================================
14. VARIABLE-LENGTH LOSSLESS CODING
======================================================================

A binary prefix code has codeword lengths l_i satisfying Kraft:

    sum_i 2^{-l_i}<=1.

Conversely, integer lengths satisfying Kraft can be realized by a prefix code.

McMillan's inequality extends the same necessary length condition to all uniquely decodable codes.

For source probabilities p_i and expected length:

    L=sum_i p_i l_i,

one has:

    L>=H(X).

Shannon lengths:

    l_i=ceil(-log2 p_i)

give:

    H(X)<=L<H(X)+1.

Block coding reduces the per-symbol overhead:

    H(X)<=L_n/n<H(X)+1/n

for iid blocks encoded using the Shannon construction.

Huffman coding minimizes expected length among symbol-by-symbol prefix codes for a known finite distribution.

Arithmetic/range coding can approach ideal fractional log-probability lengths across long sequences.

======================================================================
15. FIXED-LENGTH ALMOST-LOSSLESS SOURCE CODING
======================================================================

For iid finite-alphabet sources, if a fixed-length block code may have vanishing block error:

- rates R>H(X) are achievable;
- rates R<H(X) are not asymptotically sufficient.

Thus H(X) is also the fixed-length almost-lossless threshold.

But if zero error is required for every possible sequence in full support, the worst-case rate is generally:

    log2 |X|

bits/symbol, not H(X).

Therefore coding criterion must always be stated.

======================================================================
16. ENTROPY RATE
======================================================================

For a stochastic process:

    H_bar
    =lim_{n->infinity}(1/n)H(X_1^n)

when the limit exists.

For many stationary processes:

    H_bar
    =lim_{n->infinity}H(X_n|X_1^{n-1}).

For a stationary first-order Markov chain:

    H_bar=H(X_t|X_{t-1}).

Example:
A binary chain switches state with probability 0.1 and has uniform stationary marginal.

Then:

    H(X_t)=1,

but:

    H_bar=h2(0.1)
         ≈0.468996 bits/symbol.

Context nearly halves the irreducible rate.

======================================================================
17. STATIONARY ERGODIC SOURCES
======================================================================

The Shannon-McMillan-Breiman theorem extends the AEP beyond iid sources.

Under stationary ergodic assumptions, the normalized negative log likelihood converges to the entropy rate under standard conditions.

This supplies the foundation for compression of sources with memory.

Nonergodic sources require greater care: different components may exhibit different asymptotic information rates.

======================================================================
18. UNIVERSAL COMPRESSION
======================================================================

If p is unknown, the compressor must learn structure while encoding.

Universal coding studies codes whose redundancy relative to the best model in a class vanishes appropriately.

Important examples/ideas:

- sequential probability assignment;
- Krichevsky-Trofimov estimators;
- arithmetic coding;
- Lempel-Ziv dictionary methods.

The entropy limit is therefore distinct from the extra finite-data cost of not knowing the source law.

======================================================================
19. SLEPIAN-WOLF DISTRIBUTED SOURCE CODING
======================================================================

Two separated encoders observe correlated iid sources X^n and Y^n. They encode independently, but a joint decoder reconstructs both.

The lossless achievable region is:

    R_X >= H(X|Y),
    R_Y >= H(Y|X),
    R_X+R_Y >= H(X,Y).

This is surprising because separate encoders can asymptotically achieve the same total rate as a joint encoder.

Random binning is the key achievability idea.

======================================================================
20. DISCRETE MEMORYLESS CHANNELS
======================================================================

A DMC is described by:

    W(y|x).

For blocklength n:

    W^n(y^n|x^n)
    =product_i W(y_i|x_i).

An (n,M) code maps one of M messages to an input block and decodes from the output block.

Rate:

    R=(1/n)log2 M.

One must specify:
- average versus maximal error;
- allowed error probability;
- input constraints;
- blocklength regime.

======================================================================
21. CHANNEL CAPACITY
======================================================================

For a DMC:

    C=max_{p(x)} I(X;Y).

Operational theorem:

For every R<C, there exist sufficiently long codes with arbitrarily small block error.

For R>C, block error cannot vanish.

Thus capacity is the supremum reliable communication rate in bits per channel use under the specified model.

======================================================================
22. BINARY SYMMETRIC CHANNEL
======================================================================

BSC(epsilon):

    Y=X xor Z,
    Z~Bernoulli(epsilon).

Capacity:

    C=1-h2(epsilon).

For epsilon=0.1:

    h2(0.1)=0.4689955936,

so:

    C=0.5310044064 bits/use.

At epsilon=1/2:

    C=0.

At epsilon=1:

    C=1,

because every bit is deterministically inverted and can be flipped back.

======================================================================
23. BINARY ERASURE CHANNEL
======================================================================

BEC(delta):
a bit is erased with probability delta and otherwise received exactly.

Capacity:

    C=1-delta.

A fraction 1-delta of channel uses survive and can carry one reliable bit each asymptotically.

======================================================================
24. ASYMMETRIC CHANNELS
======================================================================

For asymmetric channels, uniform inputs need not maximize mutual information.

Example Z-channel:

    W(.|0)=(1,0),
    W(.|1)=(0.2,0.8).

Numerical optimization gives approximately:

    P(X=1)=0.435664,

and:

    C≈0.618231 bits/use.

The Blahut-Arimoto algorithm is a standard iterative method for computing DMC capacity.

======================================================================
25. CHANNEL CODING ACHIEVABILITY
======================================================================

Fix p(x) and draw approximately:

    M=2^{nR}

random codewords iid from p^n.

Use a jointly typical or likelihood-based decoder.

For an incorrect independent codeword, accidental compatibility with the observed output has probability exponentially about:

    2^{-nI(X;Y)}.

There are about:

    2^{nR}

competitors.

A union-bound heuristic yields:

    2^{-n[I(X;Y)-R]}.

Thus R<I(X;Y) permits vanishing ensemble-average error.

Optimizing over p(x) yields all R<C.

This is an existence theorem, not necessarily a practical code construction.

======================================================================
26. CHANNEL CODING CONVERSE
======================================================================

Let message W be uniform over M=2^{nR} values.

Fano:

    H(W|Y^n)
    <=h2(P_e)+P_e log(M-1).

Then:

    nR
    =I(W;Y^n)+H(W|Y^n).

Data processing:

    I(W;Y^n)<=I(X^n;Y^n).

For a DMC:

    I(X^n;Y^n)<=nC.

If P_e->0:

    R<=C.

This is the weak converse.

For ordinary finite-alphabet DMCs, stronger results show that if R>C by a fixed amount, error tends to one: the strong converse.

======================================================================
27. ERROR EXPONENTS
======================================================================

Capacity is only first-order.

At R<C, optimal error probability often behaves exponentially:

    P_e≈exp[-nE(R)].

The reliability function E(R) characterizes the best exponent.

Random-coding and sphere-packing bounds are fundamental, but exact reliability functions are not known for every channel and rate.

This is an example of a research-level boundary rather than a closed chapter.

======================================================================
28. FINITE-BLOCKLENGTH INFORMATION THEORY
======================================================================

Let R*(n,epsilon) be maximal rate at blocklength n and target error epsilon.

For many regular memoryless channels:

    R*(n,epsilon)
    =C-sqrt(V/n)Q^{-1}(epsilon)
     +O(log n/n).

V is channel dispersion, related to variance of information density at capacity.

For BSC(p):

    V=p(1-p)
      [log2((1-p)/p)]^2.

At p=0.1:

    C≈0.5310044,
    V≈0.9043582.

For epsilon=0.001, the second-order approximation gives approximately:

    n=100:   R≈0.2371
    n=1000:  R≈0.4381
    n=10000: R≈0.5016

before third-order corrections.

This shows why asymptotic capacity can substantially overstate practical short-block rate.

======================================================================
29. FEEDBACK
======================================================================

For a stationary memoryless point-to-point channel, noiseless feedback does not increase Shannon capacity.

But feedback can affect:
- error exponents;
- latency;
- variable-length performance;
- coding simplicity;
- channels with memory;
- networks.

For causal channels with feedback/memory, directed information is often the relevant information-flow quantity.

======================================================================
30. ZERO-ERROR CAPACITY
======================================================================

Vanishing-error capacity allows a small residual error that tends to zero.

Zero-error capacity requires exactly zero decoding error.

The latter becomes a graph-theoretic confusability problem and can differ sharply from Shannon capacity.

This is a warning that changing an operational criterion can change the entire theory.

======================================================================
31. COST-CONSTRAINED CAPACITY
======================================================================

If input x has cost c(x) and average cost must not exceed Gamma:

    C(Gamma)
    =max_{p(x):E[c(X)]<=Gamma}
       I(X;Y).

Power-constrained Gaussian capacity is a continuous example of this principle.

======================================================================
32. DIFFERENTIAL ENTROPY
======================================================================

For a continuous variable with density f:

    h(X)
    =-integral f(x)log2 f(x) dx.

Unlike discrete entropy:

- h(X) can be negative;
- h(aX)=h(X)+log2|a|;
- it depends on units/coordinates.

Therefore differential entropy is not an invariant absolute information content.

For small quantization step Delta:

    H(X_Delta)
    =h(X)+log2(1/Delta)+o(1)

under regularity conditions.

Relative entropy and mutual information are more invariant continuous quantities.

======================================================================
33. GAUSSIAN MAXIMUM ENTROPY
======================================================================

Among real distributions with fixed variance sigma^2, the Gaussian maximizes differential entropy:

    h(X)
    <=0.5 log2(2*pi*e*sigma^2).

One elegant proof uses nonnegativity of KL divergence between the true law and a Gaussian with matching first two moments.

======================================================================
34. AWGN CHANNEL
======================================================================

Real scalar channel:

    Y=X+N,

with:

    N~Normal(0,sigma_N^2),

independent of X and input power constraint:

    E[X^2]<=P.

Capacity:

    C
    =0.5 log2(1+P/sigma_N^2)

bits per real channel use.

Gaussian input X~Normal(0,P) achieves the maximum.

Parallel Gaussian channels lead to water-filling power allocation.

======================================================================
35. RATE-DISTORTION THEORY
======================================================================

Let d(x,xhat) measure reconstruction distortion.

For memoryless sources, define:

    R(D)
    =min_{p(xhat|x):
          E[d(X,Xhat)]<=D}
       I(X;Xhat).

Operationally, R(D) is the asymptotic minimum bits per source symbol needed for average distortion at most D under standard assumptions.

Properties:
- nonincreasing in D;
- convex in D;
- equals zero when a constant reconstruction meets the distortion constraint.

======================================================================
36. BINARY RATE-DISTORTION
======================================================================

For:

    X~Bernoulli(1/2)

with Hamming distortion:

    R(D)=1-h2(D),
    0<=D<=1/2.

For D>=1/2:

    R(D)=0.

======================================================================
37. GAUSSIAN RATE-DISTORTION
======================================================================

For:

    X~Normal(0,sigma^2)

with squared-error distortion:

    R(D)
    =0.5 log2(sigma^2/D),
    0<D<sigma^2.

For D>=sigma^2:

    R(D)=0.

======================================================================
38. SOURCE-CHANNEL SEPARATION
======================================================================

Under standard asymptotic memoryless assumptions, source compression and channel coding may be designed separately without loss of optimality.

For lossless communication, the source information rate must fit below available channel capacity.

For lossy communication at distortion D:

    R(D)

must fit below the available channel rate after accounting for source/channel use ratios.

Separation is foundational but not universally operationally optimal under strict delay, finite blocklength, or network constraints.

======================================================================
39. HYPOTHESIS TESTING
======================================================================

For iid samples distinguishing P from Q:

    log[P(X^n)/Q(X^n)]
    =sum_i log[P(X_i)/Q(X_i)].

Under P, normalized log likelihood ratio tends to:

    D(P||Q).

Stein's lemma links KL divergence to an optimal asymmetric error exponent.

Chernoff information governs a different symmetric/Bayesian exponential tradeoff.

The operational criterion determines the relevant information measure.

======================================================================
40. LARGE DEVIATIONS
======================================================================

Sanov's theorem says, roughly, that the probability an iid empirical distribution falls in a rare set A decays exponentially at a rate governed by:

    inf_{q in A} D(q||p).

Thus KL divergence quantifies the exponential improbability of empirical laws far from the truth.

======================================================================
41. MULTIPLE-ACCESS CHANNEL
======================================================================

For two independent senders and a memoryless MAC, a canonical achievable/capacity-region description for a fixed product input law contains:

    R1 <= I(X1;Y|X2),
    R2 <= I(X2;Y|X1),
    R1+R2 <= I(X1,X2;Y).

Union over admissible input laws and time sharing gives the full memoryless MAC region under standard assumptions.

This replaces one scalar capacity by a rate region.

======================================================================
42. HARDER MULTI-USER PROBLEMS
======================================================================

Broadcast and interference channels demonstrate that network information theory is not simply repeated point-to-point theory.

General capacity regions can be unknown.

This is scientifically important: a mature exposition should identify unsolved or only partially characterized regimes instead of presenting the field as closed.

======================================================================
43. SIDE INFORMATION
======================================================================

Slepian-Wolf:
lossless distributed coding with correlated decoder information.

Wyner-Ziv:
lossy coding with decoder side information.

Gel'fand-Pinsker:
channel coding when transmitter knows state noncausally.

These problems show that information structure depends on who knows which random variables and at what time.

======================================================================
44. INFORMATION SPECTRUM
======================================================================

For nonstationary, nonergodic, or channels with memory, single-letter formulas may fail.

A more general approach studies normalized random quantities such as:

    (1/n)i(X^n;Y^n)

and their probabilistic liminf/limsup behavior.

The information-spectrum framework generalizes entropy-rate and capacity ideas without demanding iid structure.

======================================================================
45. RÉNYI AND MIN-ENTROPY
======================================================================

Rényi entropy of order alpha:

    H_alpha(X)
    =(1/(1-alpha))
      log2 sum_x p(x)^alpha.

Special/limiting cases:

    alpha->1:
      Shannon entropy.

    alpha=2:
      collision entropy.

    alpha->infinity:
      min-entropy
      =-log2 max_x p(x).

These measures answer different operational questions. Shannon entropy is distinguished by average logarithmic coding and classical communication limits; min-entropy is especially relevant to worst-case randomness and cryptographic extraction.

======================================================================
46. WORKED EXAMPLE: BIASED SOURCE
======================================================================

Suppose:

    P(X=1)=0.9,
    P(X=0)=0.1.

Entropy:

    H(X)=h2(0.1)
        ≈0.468996 bits/symbol.

A naive fixed one-bit representation uses 1 bit/symbol.

Long-block lossless compression can approach approximately:

    0.469 bits/symbol

under the standard asymptotic criterion.

For one million iid symbols, the first-order information content is about:

    469,000 bits,

not counting model description, finite-block redundancy, framing, or implementation overhead.

======================================================================
47. WORKED EXAMPLE: CORRELATED BITS
======================================================================

Let X be fair and let Y be X passed through BSC(0.1).

Then:

    H(X)=H(Y)=1.

Conditional entropy:

    H(Y|X)=h2(0.1)
          ≈0.468996.

Therefore:

    I(X;Y)
    =1-h2(0.1)
    ≈0.531004 bits.

Observing Y removes about 0.531 bits of uncertainty about X on average.

======================================================================
48. WORKED EXAMPLE: MODEL MISMATCH
======================================================================

Truth:

    p=(0.9,0.1).

Model:

    q=(0.5,0.5).

True entropy:

    H(p)≈0.468996.

Cross-entropy:

    H(p,q)=1.

Penalty:

    D(p||q)
    =1-0.468996
    ≈0.531004 bits/symbol.

A wrong uniform model therefore pays about half a bit per source symbol in expected log loss.

======================================================================
49. WORKED EXAMPLE: MARKOV SOURCE
======================================================================

Binary source remains in its current state with probability 0.9 and switches with probability 0.1.

Stationary marginal:
uniform.

Single-letter entropy:

    H(X_t)=1.

Entropy rate:

    H_bar=H(X_t|X_{t-1})
         =h2(0.1)
         ≈0.468996.

The difference is predictable temporal structure.

======================================================================
50. WORKED EXAMPLE: Z-CHANNEL CAPACITY
======================================================================

Channel:

    0 -> 0 with probability 1.
    1 -> 0 with probability 0.2.
    1 -> 1 with probability 0.8.

Let q=P(X=1).

Then:

    P(Y=1)=0.8q.

Hence:

    I(X;Y)
    =h2(0.8q)-q h2(0.2).

Numerical maximization gives:

    q≈0.435664,

and:

    C≈0.618231 bits/use.

Uniform signaling is slightly suboptimal.

======================================================================
51. RESEARCH-LEVEL DISTINCTIONS TO REMEMBER
======================================================================

Do not conflate:

- surprise with entropy;
- entropy with semantic value;
- cross-entropy with entropy;
- KL divergence with a distance metric;
- correlation with dependence;
- discrete entropy with differential entropy;
- variable-length lossless coding with fixed-length almost-lossless coding;
- vanishing-error capacity with zero-error capacity;
- asymptotic capacity with short-block throughput;
- source coding redundancy with channel coding redundancy;
- memoryless formulas with general channels;
- average error with maximal error in settings where they differ;
- Shannon entropy with Rényi/min-entropy;
- probabilistic entropy with Kolmogorov complexity.

======================================================================
52. COMPACT THEOREM AND FORMULA MAP
======================================================================

Self-information:
    i(x)=-log p(x).

Entropy:
    H(X)=-sum_x p(x)log p(x).

Binary entropy:
    h2(p)=-p log p-(1-p)log(1-p).

Joint entropy:
    H(X,Y)=-sum p(x,y)log p(x,y).

Chain rule:
    H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y|X).

KL divergence:
    D(p||q)=sum p log(p/q)>=0.

Cross-entropy:
    H(p,q)=H(p)+D(p||q).

Mutual information:
    I(X;Y)
    =H(X)-H(X|Y)
    =D(p_XY||p_Xp_Y).

Data processing:
    X->Y->Z
    implies
    I(X;Z)<=I(X;Y).

Fano:
    H(W|Y)
    <=h2(P_e)+P_e log(M-1).

Kraft:
    sum 2^{-l_i}<=1.

Prefix-code expected length:
    H(X)<=L<H(X)+1
for Shannon lengths.

Fixed-length iid almost-lossless threshold:
    R=H(X).

Entropy rate:
    H_bar=lim (1/n)H(X_1^n).

Slepian-Wolf:
    R_X>=H(X|Y),
    R_Y>=H(Y|X),
    R_X+R_Y>=H(X,Y).

DMC capacity:
    C=max_{p(x)}I(X;Y).

BSC:
    C=1-h2(epsilon).

BEC:
    C=1-delta.

Finite-blocklength normal approximation:
    R*(n,epsilon)
    ≈C-sqrt(V/n)Q^{-1}(epsilon).

Cost-constrained capacity:
    C(Gamma)=max_{E[c(X)]<=Gamma}I(X;Y).

Gaussian scalar channel:
    C=0.5 log2(1+SNR).

Rate-distortion:
    R(D)
    =min_{E[d]<=D}I(X;Xhat).

Fair binary/Hamming:
    R(D)=1-h2(D).

Gaussian/squared error:
    R(D)=0.5 log2(sigma^2/D).

MAC:
    R1<=I(X1;Y|X2),
    R2<=I(X2;Y|X1),
    R1+R2<=I(X1,X2;Y).

======================================================================
53. WHAT INFORMATION THEORY DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY SOLVE
======================================================================

Classical information theory does not by itself determine:

- semantic importance of a message;
- computational feasibility of optimal codes;
- best algorithms at short blocklength;
- strict latency performance;
- behavior under arbitrary adversaries;
- privacy or fairness objectives;
- optimal network communication in every topology;
- robustness to unknown nonstationary environments.

Those problems require additional modeling and often additional theory.

======================================================================
54. CORE SYNTHESIS
======================================================================

The field can be understood as a theory of logarithmic effective multiplicity.

Independent possibilities multiply, so logarithms make their information additive.

For a source:
    2^{nH}
describes the effective number of probable length-n outcomes.

For a noisy channel:
    2^{nH(Y|X)}
describes a typical noise cloud around a codeword, while
    2^{nH(Y)}
describes the typical output space.
Their ratio has exponent:
    I(X;Y).

For lossy compression:
the source typical set is covered by distortion balls, and the number of required reproduction points has exponent R(D).

For hypothesis testing:
probabilities of atypical empirical laws decay with exponents controlled by KL divergence.

Thus compression, communication, prediction, inference, and large deviations are not separate tricks. They are different operational manifestations of the same logarithmic probability geometry.

The associated research method is equally important:

1. state the operational problem;
2. expose assumptions;
3. derive a candidate quantity from invariance/composition;
4. attack it with counterexamples;
5. seek an independent combinatorial derivation;
6. test small cases computationally;
7. prove achievability;
8. prove a converse;
9. study finite-size corrections;
10. generalize cautiously and record where the proof no longer applies.

That workflow is the research lesson behind the theory.

======================================================================
55. LOG-SUM, CONDITIONAL KL, AND WHY ONE INEQUALITY POWERS MANY RESULTS
======================================================================

The log-sum inequality states:

    sum_i a_i log(a_i/b_i)
    >=
    (sum_i a_i)
    log[
      (sum_i a_i)/(sum_i b_i)
    ].

It yields:
- KL nonnegativity;
- contraction of KL under coarse-graining;
- joint convexity of divergence;
- several data-processing arguments.

Conditional KL:

    D(P_{Y|X}||Q_{Y|X}|P_X)
    =
    sum_x P_X(x)
      D(P_{Y|X=x}||Q_{Y|X=x}).

KL chain rule:

    D(P_XY||Q_XY)
    =
    D(P_X||Q_X)
    +
    D(P_{Y|X}||Q_{Y|X}|P_X).

This is the divergence analogue of the entropy chain rule.

======================================================================
56. VARIATIONAL KL AND INFORMATION GEOMETRY
======================================================================

A useful variational representation, in natural units, is:

    D(P||Q)
    =
    sup_f {
      E_P[f]
      -
      log E_Q[e^f]
    }.

This links divergence to convex duality and large deviations.

For a smooth parametric family p_theta:

    D(
      p_theta
      ||
      p_{theta+dtheta}
    )

has a second-order expansion governed by Fisher information.

Thus:
- KL measures global mismatch;
- Fisher information describes local statistical distinguishability.

======================================================================
57. TOTAL VARIATION AND PINSKER
======================================================================

Total variation:

    TV(P,Q)
    =(1/2)||P-Q||_1.

Pinsker, using natural logs:

    D(P||Q)>=2 TV(P,Q)^2.

In bits:

    D_bits(P||Q)
    >=(2/ln 2)TV(P,Q)^2.

Hence a small KL divergence forces all event probabilities under P and Q to be close.

======================================================================
58. SOURCE-CODING SECOND ORDER
======================================================================

Let:

    V_s
    =Var[-log2 p(X)]

be varentropy.

For iid fixed-length almost-lossless compression, a second-order approximation has form:

    R*(n,epsilon)
    approx
    H(X)
    +
    sqrt(V_s/n)
    Q^{-1}(epsilon)

plus lower-order terms under standard regularity.

The plus sign matters:
a finite source code needs rate above entropy to capture all but epsilon probability mass.

For channel coding the corresponding correction is below capacity.

======================================================================
59. DISTRIBUTED SOURCE CODING PROOF LOGIC
======================================================================

Slepian-Wolf converse:

Reliable reconstruction implies, approximately:

    nR_X
    >=H(X^n|Y^n)
    =nH(X|Y),

and similarly for Y, plus:

    n(R_X+R_Y)
    >=H(X^n,Y^n).

Achievability:
randomly bin source sequences.
The decoder uses correlation to disambiguate the correct sequence inside the indicated bins.

The theorem is one of the clearest demonstrations that "information available at the decoder" can replace transmitted bits.

======================================================================
60. CAPACITY AS A DIVERGENCE RADIUS
======================================================================

For finite DMCs:

    C
    =
    min_QY max_x
      D(W(.|x)||QY).

This alternative formula characterizes capacity as the smallest divergence-radius output distribution covering all channel output laws.

It complements:

    C=max_PX I(X;Y).

The two forms reveal a minimax geometry behind capacity.

======================================================================
61. BLAHUT-ARIMOTO
======================================================================

The Blahut-Arimoto algorithm alternates between an output distribution induced by the current input law and divergence-based updates of that input law.

For the Z-channel:

    W(.|0)=(1,0)
    W(.|1)=(0.2,0.8),

it converges to:

    P(X=0)≈0.564336
    P(X=1)≈0.435664

with:

    C≈0.618231 bits/use.

It is a concrete example of turning an information-theoretic variational formula into a numerical algorithm.

======================================================================
62. AVERAGE VERSUS MAXIMAL ERROR
======================================================================

For a point-to-point code with average error epsilon, expurgating the worst half of messages leaves:
- at least half the messages;
- maximal error at most 2epsilon;
- only 1/n bit/use rate loss.

Thus average- and maximal-error capacities agree for ordinary single-user DMCs.

This equivalence should not be generalized blindly to networks.

======================================================================
63. NONASYMPTOTIC CONVERSES
======================================================================

Fano is powerful but can be loose at finite n.

Modern finite-blocklength converses often reduce decoding to binary hypothesis testing against an auxiliary output law.

The resulting bounds depend directly on likelihood ratios and information density.

This perspective explains why hypothesis testing, channel coding, and information density are mathematically intertwined.

======================================================================
64. CAPACITY PER UNIT COST
======================================================================

If symbols consume cost c(x), then ordinary capacity per use may be less informative than bits per unit energy or resource.

Under suitable zero-cost-symbol conditions, a divergence ratio of the form:

    D(W(.|x)||W(.|x0))
    /
    c(x)

governs the low-cost efficiency limit.

This gives KL divergence a direct energy-efficiency interpretation.

======================================================================
65. ENTROPY POWER
======================================================================

Entropy power turns differential entropy into a variance-like scale.

For independent continuous X,Y:

    N(X+Y)>=N(X)+N(Y).

Gaussians achieve equality.

The entropy power inequality is central to Gaussian extremal results and additive-noise converses.

======================================================================
66. I-MMSE
======================================================================

In Gaussian observation:

    Y=sqrt(gamma)X+N,

the derivative of mutual information with respect to gamma is proportional to MMSE.

Schematically in nats:

    dI/dgamma
    =(1/2)MMSE(gamma).

This provides a deep equivalence between communication information and optimal estimation.

======================================================================
67. WATER-FILLING
======================================================================

For parallel Gaussian subchannels with noise levels N_i:

    maximize
      (1/2)sum_i log2(1+P_i/N_i)

subject to:

    P_i>=0,
    sum_i P_i<=P.

KKT conditions yield:

    P_i=(mu-N_i)^+.

Power is allocated preferentially to cleaner channels.

======================================================================
68. FINITE-BLOCKLENGTH LOSSY COMPRESSION
======================================================================

Rate-distortion R(D) is first-order.

Finite-blocklength performance depends on a dispersion-like quantity based on D-tilted information.

Under regular conditions:

    R_n(D,epsilon)
    =
    R(D)
    +
    sqrt(V(D)/n)
      Q^{-1}(epsilon)
    +
    lower-order terms.

Thus source coding, channel coding, and rate-distortion all exhibit a first-order limit plus stochastic fluctuation correction.

======================================================================
69. SECRECY
======================================================================

In a wiretap setting, a message should be:
- reliably decodable by the intended receiver;
- asymptotically uninformative to an eavesdropper.

A strong secrecy criterion is:

    I(M;Z^n)->0.

For degraded memoryless wiretap channels, secrecy rates involve a difference between useful information to the legitimate receiver and leaked information to the eavesdropper.

This extends information theory from communication to controlled disclosure.

======================================================================
70. STRONG DATA PROCESSING
======================================================================

Ordinary data processing:

    I(U;Y)<=I(U;X).

Strong data processing seeks:

    I(U;Y)<=eta I(U;X)

for eta<1 determined by a noisy channel under appropriate assumptions.

It quantifies contraction rate, not merely monotonicity.

======================================================================
71. DIRECTED INFORMATION
======================================================================

For causal feedback systems:

    I(X^n -> Y^n)
    =
    sum_t I(X^t;Y_t|Y^{t-1}).

Unlike ordinary mutual information, this quantity respects temporal direction.

It is useful when channel inputs depend causally on past outputs.

======================================================================
72. INFORMATION SPECTRUM AS THE GENERAL BACKSTOP
======================================================================

Classical formulas often assume iid or stationary ergodic behavior.

When normalized information density does not converge to one constant, use its probabilistic liminf/limsup instead.

Information-spectrum theory can treat:
- nonergodic sources;
- nonstationary channels;
- channels with memory;
- mixtures.

Classical entropy and capacity become special cases.

======================================================================
73. STOCHASTIC NOISE VERSUS ADVERSARIAL ERRORS
======================================================================

A BSC with crossover probability 0.1 is not the same as an adversary allowed to corrupt any 10% of symbols.

Stochastic channels:
analyzed through probability distributions and mutual information.

Adversarial channels:
often analyzed through code distance, worst-case balls, list decoding, or arbitrarily varying channel theory.

Modeling the noise mechanism is part of the theorem.

======================================================================
74. COMPUTATION AS A SECOND RESOURCE
======================================================================

Shannon theory measures communication/storage resources while usually abstracting away computational cost.

A code may be information-theoretically optimal and computationally useless.

Practical code design therefore trades:
- gap to capacity;
- blocklength;
- decoding complexity;
- latency;
- memory;
- implementation robustness.

Capacity is a benchmark, not a complete design specification.

======================================================================
75. OPERATIONAL MAP OF INFORMATION QUANTITIES
======================================================================

Question:
How surprising was an event?
Quantity:
    -log p(x).

Question:
Average uncertainty?
Quantity:
    H(X).

Question:
Penalty for using wrong probabilistic model?
Quantity:
    D(P||Q).

Question:
How much does Y tell us about X?
Quantity:
    I(X;Y).

Question:
Minimum asymptotic lossless source rate?
Quantity:
    entropy rate.

Question:
Maximum reliable DMC rate?
Quantity:
    C=max I(X;Y).

Question:
Minimum lossy source rate at distortion D?
Quantity:
    R(D).

Question:
Best distributed lossless rates?
Quantity:
    conditional/joint entropies.

Question:
Finite-blocklength penalty?
Quantity:
    information-density variance/dispersion-like terms.

Question:
Rare empirical event exponent?
Quantity:
    KL divergence.

Question:
Cryptographic worst-case unpredictability?
Often:
    min-entropy/smooth min-entropy.

This map is preferable to saying vaguely that one number is "the information."

======================================================================
76. RESEARCH-GRADE CHECKLIST
======================================================================

Before accepting any information-theoretic statement, ask:

1. What random variables and probability laws are defined?
2. Are alphabets discrete or continuous?
3. Are support conditions satisfied?
4. Is the source iid, stationary, ergodic, Markov, or arbitrary?
5. Is the channel memoryless?
6. What error criterion is used?
7. Is the code fixed-length or variable-length?
8. Is the result zero-error, vanishing-error, or epsilon-error?
9. Is distortion average or excess-probability based?
10. Is the result asymptotic or finite-blocklength?
11. Are power/cost constraints specified?
12. Is side information present, and where?
13. Is feedback allowed?
14. Is the model known exactly?
15. Does the proof include both achievability and converse?
16. Are simulations being mistaken for proofs?
17. Are continuous-coordinate effects being ignored?
18. Are semantic/task claims being inferred from syntactic information measures without an explicit utility/distortion model?

This checklist is as important as the formula sheet.

======================================================================
78. HISTORICAL AND LITERATURE PLACEMENT
======================================================================

After the theory is derived independently, its modern placement can be identified.

Claude Shannon's 1948 paper "A Mathematical Theory of Communication" unified source statistics, logarithmic uncertainty, coding, noise, and a critical reliable communication rate. Hartley and Nyquist supplied important earlier communication-theoretic antecedents.

Later developments supplied much of the structure now regarded as graduate-level information theory:
- optimal prefix coding;
- distributed source coding;
- universal compression;
- hypothesis testing and large deviations;
- strong converses and error exponents;
- numerical capacity optimization;
- rate-distortion theory;
- feedback and network information theory;
- finite-blocklength/dispersion theory;
- secrecy and resolvability;
- general information-spectrum formulations.

A canonical modern text is Cover and Thomas, *Elements of Information Theory*. Modern graduate notes by Polyanskiy and Wu go further into variational characterizations, finite-blocklength bounds, strong converses, universal compression, and network topics.

The historical cross-check is useful only after derivation: it tells us what the independently discovered objects are called and which technical areas remain to be filled in.

======================================================================
79. FINAL META-LESSON FOR RESEARCH TRAINING
======================================================================

The most important lesson of this dataset is methodological.

A model trained only on finished formulas may learn to pattern-match.

A model trained on a disciplined research trace should instead learn to:

- turn vague engineering language into operational definitions;
- keep assumptions explicit;
- derive candidate quantities from invariance and composition;
- construct rival definitions and try to break them;
- use exact small cases before trusting asymptotics;
- use computation as a falsification and verification tool;
- reject contaminated tool runs;
- separate evidence from proof;
- independently derive the same quantity from probability, combinatorics, coding, and statistics;
- pair every achievability claim with a converse question;
- distinguish first-order asymptotics from finite-size corrections and error exponents;
- identify where a theorem stops applying;
- consult literature after independent work to validate scope and terminology;
- record open problems instead of manufacturing false closure.

That research workflow is more general than information theory itself.
